questions.question: An intoxicated patient with a head injury drifts in and out of consciousness and cannot answer questions coherently. He needs immediate care and transport. Under what principle may the crew treat him despite his inability to consent?
choices: medical direction
duty to act
emergency doctrine
implied parental consent
questions.explanation: The doctrine covers patients incapable of granting consent because of altered consciousness or the effects of drugs or alcohol.

questions.question: Donald 'Dax' Cowart, 25, was burned over about 65% of his body in a 1973 propane explosion and repeatedly demanded that painful burn treatment stop and he be allowed to die; providers treated him for 14 months anyway, relying on his mother's consent, even after a psychiatrist affirmed his capacity to decide. What does his case teach about assessing competence?
choices: Severe pain automatically makes a patient incompetent, so the family's consent should control treatment.
A refusal that will lead to the patient's death is itself proof that the patient cannot be competent.
A patient in severe pain can still be competent; assess decision-making ability directly instead of assuming disagreement means incapacity.
Crews should follow the family's wishes whenever the patient's own choice seems self-destructive.
questions.explanation: Competence is the ability to make rational decisions about one's own well-being — severe pain and an unwise-seeming refusal do not erase it.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: Decomposition of body tissues; a definitive sign of death.
choices: contributory negligence
res ipsa loquitur
putrefaction
false imprisonment
questions.explanation: putrefaction: Decomposition of body tissues; a definitive sign of death.

questions.question: In 1951, tumor tissue was taken from Henrietta Lacks during cervical cancer treatment at Johns Hopkins and given to a researcher without her knowledge or consent; her cells became the immortal HeLa line used worldwide, and her family learned of it only in the 1970s. What principle does her case establish for patient care?
choices: Consent is unnecessary for using a patient's tissue as long as the patient is not charged for the research.
A patient's family has no legitimate interest in how the patient's cells are used after treatment ends.
Tissue, blood, and information taken during care belong to the patient, not the system — obtain consent and protect patient information.
Once tissue is removed during treatment, the hospital owns it and may use it for research freely.
questions.explanation: The Lacks case is a central bioethics study of consent, tissue ownership, and fairness in health-care research.

questions.question: An unconscious trauma patient needs an airway and cannot respond. Crews treat him under the legal assumption he would want life-saving care. His care still rests on consent in which form?
choices: expressed consent
an advance directive
implied consent
informed consent
questions.explanation: Permission is presumed for a patient unable to give consent who needs emergency care — implied consent.

questions.question: You are called to check a person found in an unheated cabin. The body is stiff, blood has pooled on the underside, and the skin feels the same temperature as the cold room air. Which sign describes the body cooling to match the room?
choices: algor mortis
rigor mortis
putrefaction
livor mortis
questions.explanation: Algor mortis is the cooling of the body after death until it matches the ambient temperature.

questions.question: A paramedic performs a skill that state law reserves to a higher certification level, and the patient is harmed by exactly the complication the certification law was written to prevent. The plaintiff's attorney says no separate proof of carelessness is needed because the statute was broken. This argument is:
choices: negligence per se
comparative negligence
contributory negligence
vicarious liability
questions.explanation: When conduct clearly violates a statute designed to prevent that type of harm, the violation itself can establish negligence under negligence per se.

questions.question: What does the term "patient autonomy" mean?
choices: The seizing, confining, abducting, or carrying away of a person by force, including transporting a competent adult for medical treatment against his or her will.
The right of a patient to make informed choices regarding his or her health care.
Written, accepted levels of emergency care expected by reason of training and profession; written by legal or professional organizations so that patients are not exposed to unreasonable risk or harm.
The study of ethics related to issues that arise in health care.
questions.explanation: patient autonomy: The right of a patient to make informed choices regarding his or her health care.

questions.question: An EMT is subpoenaed to testify about a run report while a forensic pathologist testifies about autopsy findings in the same trial. The EMT's supervisor calls it a classic example of what kind of case?
choices: contractual
humanitarian
administrative
medicolegal
questions.explanation: A case combining medical care and documentation with legal proceedings and forensic medicine is a medicolegal case.

questions.question: What does the term "bioethics" mean?
choices: A type of advance directive executed by a competent adult that appoints another individual to make medical treatment decisions on his or her behalf when he or she is unable to do so.

Legal doctrine that can protect an EMS provider from being sued or that may limit the amount of the monetary judgement (the amount of money that a court of law orders one person to pay to another) against the EMS provider.
The study of ethics related to issues that arise in health care.
The time within which a legal case must be commenced.
questions.explanation: bioethics: The study of ethics related to issues that arise in health care.

questions.question: Which finding best supports that a patient has decision-making capacity to refuse care?
choices: The patient can explain the condition, the proposed treatment, and the risks of refusing in his own words
The patient is alert and can state his name, address, and date of birth
A family member at the scene supports the patient's decision to refuse
The patient agrees with the crew's recommendation to be transported
questions.explanation: Capacity is shown by understanding and processing information and making a choice, not by agreeing with the crew.

questions.question: A 16-year-old who lives at home, attends high school, and is fully supported by his parents says, 'I'm emancipated, I can refuse.' What should the EMT do?
choices: Accept his refusal — a teenager who claims emancipation must be taken at his word
Treat him as a minor — seek parental consent / medical control, because those facts do not show emancipation
Accept his refusal — any patient over 15 may refuse transport on scene
Transport him against his will without contacting anyone, because minors have no say in their care
questions.explanation: An emancipated minor needs qualifying circumstances such as marriage, military service, court order, or independent living; living at home supported by parents is the opposite.

questions.question: After a car crashes into a light pole at about 45 mph, a bystander who fears the car will catch fire pulls her friend from the front passenger seat; the friend is left permanently paralyzed, and a court holds the Good Samaritan statute covered only emergency medical care, which the bystander did not claim to have rendered. What is the lesson for responders?
choices: Good Samaritan law protects every helpful act at a crash scene, medical or not.
Bystanders should never touch a crash victim under any circumstances.
Always remove crash victims from the vehicle immediately, whatever the hazard.
Move a crash victim only for a real hazard when you can, and use spinal precautions; your protection depends on the care actually being emergency care in good faith.
questions.explanation: Good Samaritan protection covers good faith emergency care as the statute defines it, not every helpful act at a scene.

questions.question: Mary Schloendorff was admitted to a New York hospital in 1908 and consented only to an examination under ether, expressly declining surgery; while she was anesthetized, surgeons removed a tumor anyway, and Judge Cardozo later wrote that every adult of sound mind has the right to determine what shall be done with his own body. What does this case establish about consent?
choices: Consent for one procedure is not consent for another; when a patient says no, treatment beyond that permission is an unlawful touching — battery.
A surgeon may extend an operation whenever the finding is serious, because consent to anesthesia covers it.
The unauthorized surgery is only negligence, because the surgeon intended to help the patient.
Consent given for an examination implies consent to any treatment the examination happens to reveal.
questions.explanation: Schloendorff is the foundation of medical battery law: operating without the patient's consent is an unlawful touching, however well intended.

questions.question: A diabetic patient sues after a hypoglycemia call, and the defense presents evidence that she repeatedly skipped insulin and ignored discharge instructions before the call. The defense is best described as what?
choices: contributory negligence
statute of limitations
assumption of the risk
gross negligence
questions.explanation: The defense is built on the plaintiff's own conduct contributing to the harm claimed in the lawsuit.

questions.question: After a difficult call, a paramedic tells the receiving staff, within earshot of other patients, that the patient 'is just a drug-seeking faker,' and the statement is untrue. The patient, a schoolteacher, is later shunned by coworkers who heard about it. What tort is the patient most likely to allege?
choices: defamation (slander)
battery
abandonment
breach of confidentiality
questions.explanation: False spoken information damaging a person's reputation is defamation; spoken defamation is slander.

questions.question: You arrive to find a patient with obvious dependent lividity and rigor mortis, and a detective asks you not to move the body or remove the IV your partner started. He says the death is now a medical examiner's case. Which term describes this blend of medicine and law?
choices: prophylactic
therapeutic
medicolegal
clinical
questions.explanation: Medicolegal refers to medical jurisprudence and forensic medicine, which includes medical examiner death investigations.

questions.question: Two EMTs disagree after a call: one says taking a patient's leftover pain medication home is stealing and wrong in itself, even if no rule were ever enforced. He is appealing to what?
choices: protocol
customary practice
civil liability
morality
questions.explanation: Judging an act as right or wrong by an internal and societal code of conduct, not just by rules or law, is morality.

questions.question: Assessment in Action: On another call that day, your patient consented to treatment and transport after you told her she could be experiencing a serious medical emergency. This is an example of:
choices: scope of practice.
implied consent.
serving in the patient’s best interest.
an EMS field impression.
questions.explanation: From the book's printed answer key.

questions.question: An EMT deliberately trips a rude bystander, who breaks a wrist and sues for damages. The bystander's claim for this intentional wrongful act is best classified as what?
choices: a breach of contract claim
an intentional tort
a workers' compensation claim
a criminal assault charge
questions.explanation: Intentional wrongful acts such as battery are torts and are pursued as civil lawsuits.

questions.question: An EMT begins an IV on a competent patient who has just said, 'No needles, I do not want that.' Continuing anyway most directly violates what?
choices: duty to act
confidentiality
patient autonomy
expressed consent
questions.explanation: Treatment imposed after a competent patient has made an informed refusal overrides the patient's right to decide about his own care.

questions.question: At a shooting scene, you cut off the victim's shirt to treat him. An officer asks you to hand the shirt to the evidence technician and sign a form listing everyone who handled it. What is that form maintaining?
choices: continuity of care
chain of evidence
chain of command
chain of survival
questions.explanation: The signed record of every person who collected, handled, and transferred the item is the chain of evidence (chain of custody).

questions.question: At trial, an expert testifies about what a reasonably trained paramedic would have done for a chest-pain patient in the same circumstances. What is the expert describing?
choices: scope of practice
standard of care
peer review
standing orders
questions.explanation: Liability is judged against the care expected by reason of training and profession, not against the individual provider's personal habits.

questions.question: An EMT handles a disputed non-emergency ambulance transport for a physician's patient. The physician sends identical seven-page complaint letters about the EMT, headed 'Abuse of Authority,' to the state governor and a member of Congress. The EMT sues the physician for defamation, but Maryland's highest court holds the letters were absolutely privileged. What is the lesson for EMS providers?
choices: Once a statement is privileged, the same protection covers repeating it anywhere, including on social media.
Government officials may not receive complaints about EMS providers without the provider's permission.
Any written complaint about a provider is automatically defamation and can be sued over successfully.
Complaints about a provider made through official channels may be privileged, but that protection disappears when statements are spread outside those channels or made with malice.
questions.explanation: Complaints made through official channels may be privileged; the protection disappears outside those channels or with malice.

questions.question: A 57-year-old Jehovah's Witness arrives unconscious after a severe car crash. She carries a signed card stating she refuses blood transfusions under any circumstances. Believing a transfusion is necessary to save her life, her physician gives blood anyway, and she recovers. The Ontario Court of Appeal upholds a $20,000 battery judgment against the physician. What does this case teach EMS providers?
choices: An unconscious patient's prior statements about treatment carry no legal weight.
The emergency doctrine overrides any refusal a patient documented while competent.
Check wallets, wristbands, and paperwork on unconscious patients, because a known advance refusal limits what emergency implied consent allows you to do.
A refusal card is valid only if it was signed and witnessed on the day of the emergency.
questions.explanation: The emergency doctrine assumes a patient would consent, and that assumption is destroyed by a known refusal.

questions.question: What does the term "morality" mean?
choices: A code of conduct that can be defined by society, religion, or a person, affecting character, conduct, and conscience.
The federal law, enacted in 1996, that protects the privacy and security of a patient's health information and limits how EMS personnel may use or share it.
The written or electronic legal record of an EMS call, which courts treat as a reflection of the care itself, so that an incomplete or untidy report is read as evidence of inadequate care.
A person who is under the legal age in a given state but, because of other circumstances, is legally considered an adult.
questions.explanation: morality: A code of conduct that can be defined by society, religion, or a person, affecting character, conduct, and conscience.

questions.question: During transport of an incapacitated stroke patient, a daughter says, 'Mom signed papers years ago saying no ventilator if she couldn't recover.' You should ask for and transport which type of document?
choices: organ donor registration card
do not resuscitate order
durable power of attorney for health care
advance directive
questions.explanation: That description matches a living will, a form of advance directive specifying future treatment.

questions.question: What does the term "negligence" mean?
choices: Failure to provide the same care that a person with similar training would provide.
A type of advance directive executed by a competent adult that appoints another individual to make medical treatment decisions on his or her behalf when he or she is unable to do so.
Wrongful acts that give rise to a civil lawsuit.
A written document that specifies medical treatment for a competent patient, should he or she become unable to make decisions in the future; also known as an advance directive or a living will.
questions.explanation: negligence: Failure to provide the same care that a person with similar training would provide.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: Immediate care or treatment.
choices: emergency medical care
contributory negligence
informed consent
assault
questions.explanation: emergency medical care: Immediate care or treatment.

questions.question: From 1932 to 1972, the U.S. Public Health Service studied about 600 African American men near Tuskegee, Alabama, including 399 with syphilis. The men were told only that they had 'bad blood,' were never given their diagnosis, and received placebos disguised as care. Even after penicillin became the standard cure by 1947, researchers withheld it to keep watching the disease progress. Press exposure ended the study in 1972, and it led to the Belmont Report and institutional review boards. What principle does this case illustrate for an EMT?
choices: Following an official program as written protects a provider from any moral responsibility for the outcome.
A practice being official, common, or ordered does not make it moral; if an order violates your conscience and harms a patient, speak up through channels.
Withholding a known cure is acceptable whenever researchers judge the scientific value to be high enough.
Patients who accept free care and exams have effectively consented to whatever treatment decisions follow.
questions.explanation: Morality is a code of right and wrong that can condemn even official, ordered conduct.

questions.question: A Kentucky paramedic treats a zookeeper bitten by a breeding mamba snake. He knows antivenom is the correct treatment and gives it during the helicopter flight, saving the patient's life, even though administering it was outside his authorized scope on paper. The state EMS board investigates him for acting beyond his authorization, then dismisses the investigation. What is the main lesson of this case for EMS providers?
choices: When a board investigates, the provider should avoid discussing the case with the medical director until the review is over.
Scope-of-practice rules never apply when a patient's life is at stake, so no documentation of the decision is necessary.
Know your protocols cold, but also know the review process: document everything and be ready to defend a life-first decision to your medical director and board.
A provider should never act outside the written scope of practice, even when doing so is the only way to save a life.
questions.explanation: Document everything and be ready to defend a life-first decision to your medical director and board.

questions.question: Mid-transport, a competent patient who first consented now demands to be let out at the next safe stop and tries to unbuckle the straps. A crew member holds her down and orders the driver to keep going to the hospital. What does continuing the transport risk being charged as?
choices: kidnapping
abandonment
assault
battery
questions.explanation: Confining and carrying away a competent person by force after consent is withdrawn, for treatment she no longer wants, fits the definition of kidnapping.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: The act of physically preventing an individual from initiating any physical action.
choices: battery
depositions
interrogatories
forcible restraint
questions.explanation: forcible restraint: The act of physically preventing an individual from initiating any physical action.

questions.question: A paramedic's spouse asks how the mayor, who was transported last shift, is doing. The paramedic shares the mayor's diagnosis and condition at home. What is this?
choices: defamation
gross negligence
libel
breach of confidentiality
questions.explanation: Telling anyone not involved in care, including family at home, discloses information without the patient's authorization.

questions.question: An off-duty EMT drives past a crash in another state where she has no assignment or employment duty. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: She is legally barred from helping because the crash is outside her jurisdiction
She must stop and begin care, but she may leave the scene whenever she chooses
She generally has no legal duty to act, but if she begins care she must continue until relieved by equal or higher care
She has the same legal duty to stop and treat as an on-duty crew in her own district
questions.explanation: Duty to act comes from statute or function; a voluntary start creates a duty not to abandon the patient.

questions.question: A man is severely brain-injured in a truck accident, conscious but unable to communicate consistently, and dependent on tube feeding. He left no health care instructions and never appointed an agent under a durable power of attorney for health care. His wife, as conservator, seeks to withhold tube feeding, but his mother and sister object, and the state supreme court limits her authority. What does this case show about decision-making authority?
choices: The crew should follow the majority vote of the family members present at the scene.
The closest relative automatically gains full authority to withhold treatment.
A conservator can always withhold artificial nutrition and hydration on a patient's behalf.

Without a durable power of attorney for health care appointing an agent, a decision-maker's authority is sharply limited, so crews should escalate to medical control rather than taking one relative's word as authority.
questions.explanation: Because no document appointed an agent, the conservator lacked authority to withhold artificial nutrition without clear and convincing evidence of the patient's wishes.
questions.topic: durable power of attorney for health care

questions.question: A woman is left in a persistent vegetative state after a car crash and is fed through a surgically placed tube. Her parents ask the hospital to remove the tube, but the hospital refuses without a court order, and the U.S. Supreme Court holds the state may require clear and convincing evidence of the patient's wishes before life support is withdrawn. Her wishes were later proven through additional evidence from friends. What practice does this case support for EMS crews?
choices: Rely on the family's verbal account alone, since relatives always know the patient's wishes best.
Treat tube feeding as a family decision that relatives may reverse at any time.
Withhold all care from incapacitated patients until a judge rules on their wishes.
Locate, copy, and transport any written directive with the patient, because oral family claims are weaker proof of the patient's wishes.
questions.explanation: A competent person's wishes, shown through a living will or other clear evidence, control — making written advance directives the strongest proof.

questions.question: You find a 24-year-old man unconscious in a crashed car with a compromised airway and no identification or family on scene. You insert an airway adjunct and begin ventilations. What legal principle permits this treatment without his consent?
choices: informed consent
Good Samaritan protection
expressed consent
emergency doctrine
questions.explanation: The emergency doctrine permits treatment in an emergency when the patient is incapable of granting consent, here because he is unconscious.

questions.question: What does the term "medicolegal" mean?
choices: The confinement of a person without legal authority or the person's consent.
Unlawfully placing a patient in fear of bodily harm.
A term relating to medical jurisprudence (law) or forensic medicine.
Type of consent in which a patient who is unable to give consent is given treatment under the legal assumption that he or she would want treatment.
questions.explanation: medicolegal: A term relating to medical jurisprudence (law) or forensic medicine.

questions.question: What does the term "dependent lividity" mean?
choices: Oral questions asked of parties and witnesses under oath.
The written or electronic legal record of an EMS call, which courts treat as a reflection of the care itself, so that an incomplete or untidy report is read as evidence of inadequate care.
Blood settling to the lowest point of the body, causing discoloration of the skin; a definitive sign of death.
A serious situation, such as injury or illness that threatens the life or welfare of a person or group of people and requires immediate intervention.
questions.explanation: dependent lividity: Blood settling to the lowest point of the body, causing discoloration of the skin; a definitive sign of death.

questions.question: An EMT asks a competent patient, 'Can I start an IV in your arm?' The patient holds out her arm toward the EMT and says nothing, but a bystander says, 'She doesn't want that.' What should the EMT do before starting the IV?
choices: implied consent (proceed, because holding out her arm already authorizes the IV)
expressed consent (confirm the patient's own verbal or nonverbal authorization directly with the patient)
obtain consent from the bystander as the patient's representative
accept the bystander's refusal and cancel the IV without asking the patient
questions.explanation: Expressed consent must come from the patient herself, verbally or nonverbally; a conflicting third-party statement means the EMT must confirm her authorization directly.

questions.question: You arrive at a home where a hospice patient is pulseless. The family says 'she never wanted CPR' but cannot produce any signed order or DNR bracelet. What is your correct action?
choices: provide comfort measures only while the family searches for the paperwork
withhold resuscitation because the family has clearly stated her wishes
begin resuscitation (no valid do not resuscitate order present)
contact the family physician by phone before deciding whether to start CPR
questions.explanation: Without the written physician documentation that defines a DNR order, verbal family statements alone do not authorize withholding resuscitation.

questions.question: What does the term "Good Samaritan laws" mean?
choices: Ability to understand and process information and make a choice regarding appropriate medical care.

Statutory provisions enacted by many states to protect citizens from liability for errors and omissions in giving good faith emergency medical care, unless there is wanton, gross, or willful negligence.
The documented, unbroken record of everyone who collected, handled, and transferred physical evidence from a crime scene, maintained so the evidence stays usable in court.
The philosophy of right and wrong, of moral duties, and of ideal professional behavior.
questions.explanation: Good Samaritan laws: Statutory provisions enacted by many states to protect citizens from liability for errors and omissions in giving good faith emergency medical care, unless there is wanton, gross, or willful negligence.

questions.question: In 1975, 21-year-old Karen Ann Quinlan remained in a persistent vegetative state on a respirator after cardiac arrest. Her Catholic parents asked that the respirator be removed so she could die naturally, but her doctors and hospital refused, fearing it could be homicide. In 1976 the New Jersey Supreme Court held that her right to refuse treatment could be exercised by her family on her behalf, writing that such decisions must respond to 'the common moral judgment of the community at large.' What should an EMT take from this case?
choices: A respirator decision is purely a legal question, so the family's values never need to be considered.
When a family disagrees with physicians, the EMT should side with whichever party asks first on scene.
End-of-life conflicts are moral as well as legal, so learn the patient's and family's values and involve medical control and the receiving facility early.
Religious beliefs of a family have no place in treatment decisions and should not be documented.
questions.explanation: The court tied its ruling to the community's moral judgment and the family's religious code, not just to law.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: When a person who has a duty abuses it, and causes harm to another individual, the EMT, the agency, and/or the medical director may be sued for negligence.
choices: negligence per se
proximate causation
rigor mortis
punitive damages
questions.explanation: proximate causation: When a person who has a duty abuses it, and causes harm to another individual, the EMT, the agency, and/or the medical director may be sued for negligence.

questions.question: A hospital forms a committee to weigh whether continuing life support for a patient with no chance of recovery is morally right, separate from what is legally allowed. What is this committee studying?
choices: malpractice law
medical jurisprudence
bioethics
risk management
questions.explanation: Applying ethical principles to a health-care dilemma is bioethics, distinct from the purely legal analysis.

questions.question: An EMT is torn between a family's plea to 'do everything' and a valid DNR the patient signed. Working through what she morally ought to do is an exercise in what?
choices: quality improvement
ethics
risk management
standard of care
questions.explanation: Weighing moral duties and right versus wrong in professional conduct is ethics.

questions.question: What does the term "putrefaction" mean?
choices: The philosophy of right and wrong, of moral duties, and of ideal professional behavior.
Conduct that constitutes a willful or reckless disregard for a duty or standard of care.
Decomposition of body tissues; a definitive sign of death.
A legal defense that may be raised when the defendant thinks that the conduct of the plaintiff somehow contributed to any injuries or damages that were sustained by the plaintiff.
questions.explanation: putrefaction: Decomposition of body tissues; a definitive sign of death.

questions.question: Your class is discussing the Tuskegee study, Quinlan, and Schiavo as examples of moral questions about consent, research, and end-of-life care in medicine. What field of study covers these issues?
choices: health-care administration
medical law
clinical research methodology
bioethics
questions.explanation: Bioethics is the study of ethics related to issues that arise in health care, and all three cases are landmark examples.

questions.question: An alert patient demands to be let out of the ambulance at a red light. The crew, with no involuntary hold and no sign the patient is a danger, locks the doors and continues to the hospital. This confinement is best described as what?
choices: false imprisonment
assault
defamation
kidnapping
questions.explanation: The patient was confined without legal authority or consent, which defines false imprisonment.

questions.question: Congress enacted EMTALA in 1986 after emergency departments were found refusing to treat indigent and uninsured patients or transferring them inappropriately — 'patient dumping'; the law requires Medicare-participating hospitals to screen anyone who comes to the emergency department and to stabilize an emergency condition or arrange an appropriate transfer. What does EMTALA require of you on an emergency call?
choices: EMTALA's screening and stabilization duties apply only to patients who arrive by ambulance.
Hospitals may transfer uninsured patients before screening whenever another facility is nearby.
Ability to pay may be verified first, provided a screening examination eventually takes place.
Your duty on an emergency call does not depend on the patient's insurance or address; screen, stabilize, and document.
questions.explanation: EMTALA guarantees emergency medical care in practice: immediate screening and stabilization first, payment questions later.

questions.question: A plaintiff's attorney wants to ask the treating paramedic questions under oath before trial to learn what she saw on scene, rather than sending written questions. What should the attorney schedule?
choices: a subpoena duces tecum
interrogatories
an evidentiary hearing
a deposition
questions.explanation: Oral questions under oath are depositions; written questions would be interrogatories.

questions.question: A walk-in patient with crushing chest pain is told at a hospital desk to sit and wait for insurance verification before anyone examines him. Which EMTALA principle about emergency medical care is violated?
choices: emergency medical care (screening and stabilization must come first, regardless of ability to pay)
emergency medical care (insurance verification is a required first step)
hospital registration policy (paperwork must be completed before screening)
patient financial counseling (payment screening precedes examination)
questions.explanation: EMTALA requires immediate screening and stabilizing care before payment questions, which is the guarantee behind emergency medical care.

questions.question: What does the term "assault" mean?
choices: Unlawfully placing a patient in fear of bodily harm.
Type of consent in which a patient who is unable to give consent is given treatment under the legal assumption that he or she would want treatment.
Immediate care or treatment.
A written document that specifies medical treatment for a competent patient, should he or she become unable to make decisions in the future; also known as an advance directive or a living will.
questions.explanation: assault: Unlawfully placing a patient in fear of bodily harm.

questions.question: Four paramedics respond to a 30-year-old woman, recently postpartum, found unconscious on a call classified as a stroke. They take no vital signs, perform no appropriate exam, suggest she has had too much to drink, and leave after about 13 minutes, reporting no patient found. Her mother drives her to the hospital, where a scan shows an acute subarachnoid hemorrhage; she dies days later, and the county settles for about $2.75 million. What standard should govern a non-transport decision?
choices: A non-transport decision needs a full assessment, vital signs, a capacity check, documentation, and medical-control involvement — never a walk-away.
A brief scene time is acceptable whenever the patient does not request transport.
If a patient appears intoxicated, crews may clear the scene without taking vital signs.
Family members can be left to transport any patient the crew judges stable enough.
questions.explanation: Leaving a patient who has not competently refused, without arranging continuing care by an equal or higher provider, is abandonment in operational form.

questions.question: A 6-year-old is pulled from a pool, apneic and pulseless, with no parent anywhere on scene. The crew begins CPR immediately. Their authority to treat without parental consent comes from:
choices: the Good Samaritan law
emergency doctrine
telephone consent
standing orders
questions.explanation: The emergency doctrine permits emergency treatment when a patient cannot consent because of age and incapacity and no surrogate is available.

questions.question: A paramedic does not restrain a delirious patient who has twice tried to exit the moving ambulance; the patient opens the door, falls out, and is killed. A jury could find the failure to restrain was what of the death?
choices: evidence of gross negligence only
the proximate cause
an unavoidable accident
a contributing factor with no legal significance
questions.explanation: The foreseeable harm flowed directly from the breach of the duty to restrain, satisfying proximate causation.

questions.question: Paramedics bring in an unconscious 70-year-old man whose chest is tattooed 'Do Not Resuscitate,' with 'Not' underlined and what appears to be his signature. No signed state DNR form has been found yet. What does the tattoo mean for withholding CPR?
choices: A tattoo alone is not a legal DNR order; look for the valid signed state DNR form or bracelet and verify it before withholding resuscitation.
Start CPR but stop it as soon as any family member arrives and objects
Ignore the tattoo entirely, because a tattoo can never reflect a patient's wishes
Honor the tattoo immediately and withhold CPR without any further verification
questions.explanation: A tattoo is not the written physician documentation a DNR requires; the valid signed order must be located before resuscitation is withheld.

questions.question: In your patient care report you write that a patient is 'a known drug dealer who faked his chest pain,' which is untrue, and the report is shared with the hospital and your agency. The patient sues. What is the written false statement called?
choices: slander
battery
perjury
libel
questions.explanation: Libel is false and damaging information about a person communicated in writing, and a patient care report is a written record.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: A type of advance directive executed by a competent adult that appoints another individual to make medical treatment decisions on his or her behalf when he or she is unable to do so.
choices: durable power of attorney for health care
battery
do not resuscitate order
applied ethics
questions.explanation: durable power of attorney for health care: A type of advance directive executed by a competent adult that appoints another individual to make medical treatment decisions on his or her behalf when he or she is unable to do so.
questions.topic: durable power of attorney for health care

questions.question: At an elementary school, a 9-year-old falls and may have a broken arm. His parents are unreachable, and the school nurse directs care and rides in the ambulance. Under what doctrine is the school acting?
choices: implied consent
emancipated minor status
duty to act
in loco parentis
questions.explanation: The school has taken on some functions and responsibilities of a parent while the child is in its care.

questions.question: After a school shooting that killed 20 first-graders and 6 adults, a broadcaster repeatedly stated on his show that the massacre was a hoax and the grieving families were 'crisis actors.' The families sued, and a jury ordered him to pay $965 million. What does this case illustrate about spoken statements?
choices: A large verdict is possible only when the speaker earned money directly from each individual statement.
Defamation requires the false statement to appear in print, so remarks made on a radio show are safe.
Spoken words are not harmless because they are 'just talking'; statements made on air, on a recorded line, or in public about patients and families can be defamation.
Statements made by broadcasters are opinions and can never support a defamation claim.
questions.explanation: False statements delivered by spoken word to a wide audience are slander, and the damages can be enormous.

questions.question: A 29-year-old woman came to a hospital during a severe asthma attack, refused intubation, and tried to leave. Staff apprehended her, placed her in four-point restraints, and intubated her about 45 minutes later over her vigorous objections. The state's highest court held the jury instructions on refusal and false imprisonment were erroneous. What principle does this case establish?
choices: A patient who initially seeks care gives implied consent to all later treatment.
Restraints applied in a hospital can never support a false imprisonment claim.
A competent adult may refuse even life-saving care; restraining and treating over that refusal risks false imprisonment liability.
In a true emergency, a competent patient's refusal can always be overridden by staff.
questions.explanation: A competent patient's refusal cannot simply be overridden in an emergency; confinement without consent is false imprisonment.

questions.question: What does the term "expressed consent" mean?
choices: A type of consent in which a patient gives verbal or nonverbal authorization for provision of care or transport.

The principle of law that permits a health care provider to treat a patient in an emergency situation when the patient is incapable of granting consent because of an altered level of consciousness, disability, the effects of drugs or alcohol, or the patient's age.
The manner in which principles of ethics are incorporated into professional conduct.
The philosophy of right and wrong, of moral duties, and of ideal professional behavior.
questions.explanation: expressed consent: A type of consent in which a patient gives verbal or nonverbal authorization for provision of care or transport.

questions.question: You find a bullet casing in the ambulance after transporting a gunshot patient. You place it in a labeled bag, seal it, and document the time, where you found it, and the officer you gave it to. What are you preserving?
choices: chain of evidence
chain of command
evidence-based practice
chain of survival
questions.explanation: Labeling, sealing, and documenting each transfer keeps the record of custody unbroken from discovery to court.

questions.question: After restraining a patient, which practice keeps forcible restraint safest: leaving him prone and hog-tied for transport, or moving him supine or seated with continuous breathing monitoring?
choices: forcible restraint done safely requires repositioning and continuous monitoring
forcible restraint done safely requires leaving him prone and hog-tied for transport
forcible restraint requires keeping the patient face-down until hospital arrival
forcible restraint is safest when the patient is left unmonitored to settle down
questions.explanation: Prone, prolonged forcible restraint has caused repeated asphyxia deaths; repositioning and monitoring are the safeguards.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: A legal defense that may be raised when the defendant thinks that the conduct of the plaintiff somehow contributed to any injuries or damages that were sustained by the plaintiff.
choices: contributory negligence
durable power of attorney for health care
health care proxy
consent
questions.explanation: contributory negligence: A legal defense that may be raised when the defendant thinks that the conduct of the plaintiff somehow contributed to any injuries or damages that were sustained by the plaintiff.

questions.question: YOU are the Provider (32-year-old man, severe headache): How does informed consent differ from implied consent?
choices: Informed consent is permission granted by medical control over the radio, while implied consent is permission granted by the patient's family members at the scene.
Informed consent applies only to minors whose parents have been notified, while implied consent applies to adults who refuse to answer the crew's questions.
Informed consent is given in writing on a signed form, while implied consent is given verbally by a conscious patient who nods or extends an arm for a blood pressure check.

Informed consent means the patient is told the nature of the illness, the treatment, its risks and benefits, alternatives, and consequences, and then gives consent. Implied consent is assumed when a patient is unconscious, confused, seriously injured, or otherwise unable to communicate in a life-threatening situation, and would consent if able.
questions.explanation: From the book's printed YOU are the Provider summary.

questions.question: A 19-year-old agreed to back surgery for a suspected ruptured disc. His surgeon did not disclose the roughly 1% risk of paralysis, later testifying he did not want to deter the patient from having the operation. The patient was left paralyzed, and the appeals court set a 'prudent patient' standard for disclosure. What does this case require of providers?
choices: Withholding a risk is acceptable whenever the provider sincerely believes the treatment is necessary.
A risk of about 1 percent is too small to ever require disclosure to the patient.
Explain the serious risks of procedures and refusals even when the explanation might make the patient decline; disclosure is judged by what a reasonable patient would find material to the decision.
Disclosure is measured by what other providers customarily mention, not by what the patient would want to know.
questions.explanation: Consent is not informed when a material risk is deliberately withheld from the patient.

questions.question: An intoxicated patient with a head injury slurs, cannot tell you where he is, and keeps saying 'let me go' without grasping that he could bleed internally. Can he validly refuse transport?
choices: Yes — his repeated request to leave counts as a valid refusal
Yes — the refusal becomes valid once he signs the refusal form
No — he lacks decision-making capacity
Yes — any adult patient may refuse care for any reason
questions.explanation: He cannot understand and process information about his care, so he cannot make a valid refusal and should be treated under implied consent with medical control / law enforcement help as needed.

questions.question: Students wore black armbands to school to protest a war, and the school, acting in place of the parents to discipline them, suspended them under a ban on armbands. The Supreme Court sided with the students. What does this show about a school's parental-style authority?
choices: A school official on scene can act for a child, but that in loco parentis authority has limits; for medical consent questions, verify who actually holds parental rights.
School staff have no authority of any kind over students and cannot speak for a child at all.
A school's authority over a child completely replaces the parents' rights until graduation.
School staff hold unlimited parental authority over students during school hours.
questions.explanation: Consent and authority on school calls: the school acts in place of parents, but that power is limited, so verify who holds parental rights.

questions.question: A paramedic discovers her partner charted a medication he never gave. Her agency's ethical standards require honesty in documentation, so she reports it to her supervisor even though it may cost her partner his job. Her action best demonstrates:
choices: peer review
quality improvement
chain of command
applied ethics
questions.explanation: She incorporated an ethical principle, honesty, into her actual professional conduct rather than just knowing the rule.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: Unlawfully placing a patient in fear of bodily harm.
choices: assault
dependent lividity
Good Samaritan laws
chain of evidence
questions.explanation: assault: Unlawfully placing a patient in fear of bodily harm.

questions.question: Attackers enter a health insurer's systems through spear-phishing emails and steal data on almost 79 million people, including names, Social Security numbers, medical ID numbers, addresses, and birth dates. The company pays $16 million, then the largest HIPAA settlement in history. Why was this data protected health information?
choices: Data taken by hackers is excluded from HIPAA breach rules
Only handwritten clinical notes qualify as protected health information
Insurance ID numbers are not PHI because the health plan issues them
PHI includes identifiers plus payment and coverage data, not just clinical notes.
questions.explanation: Names and medical ID numbers linked to health plan records are protected health information.

questions.question: What does the term "competent" mean?
choices: Able to make rational decisions about personal well-being.
A written document that specifies medical treatment for a competent patient, should he or she become unable to make decisions in the future; also known as an advance directive or a living will.
Unlawfully placing a patient in fear of bodily harm.
A serious situation, such as injury or illness that threatens the life or welfare of a person or group of people and requires immediate intervention.
questions.explanation: competent: Able to make rational decisions about personal well-being.

questions.question: Your patient is a 17-year-old who is married, lives with her spouse, and works full time. She is alert and refuses transport after a minor crash. How is she most likely classified for consent purposes?
choices: a minor with implied consent
a mature minor by age alone
emancipated minor
an unemancipated minor
questions.explanation: Marriage and independent adult life legally make an underage person an adult for medical decisions in most states.

questions.question: At a shooting scene, an EMT finds a boy cold and stiff on a bed with dependent lividity on the back of his body, the backs of both arms, and the lower extremities hanging off the bed, while the second victim is still warm. What does the lividity tell the EMT?
choices: A cold, stiff patient with lividity should still receive full CPR until hospital arrival.
Checking for dependent lividity is part of confirming death on scene; where it sits tells you the position the body has been in.
The warm second victim proves both victims died at the same time.
Lividity on the back proves the body was moved after death in every case.
questions.explanation: The settling pattern matched the position the body was found in, confirming he had been dead in that position for some time.

questions.question: At trial, an ambulance service argues that a trauma patient who was not wearing a seat belt and was intoxicated helped cause the severity of his own injuries, so damages should be reduced or barred. This argument is an example of what?
choices: comparative fault immunity
res ipsa loquitur
assumption of the risk
contributory negligence
questions.explanation: The defendant is asserting that the plaintiff's conduct contributed to his own injuries or damages.

questions.question: What does the term "breach of confidentiality" mean?
choices: Disclosure of information without proper authorization.
The right of a patient to make informed choices regarding his or her health care.
A term relating to medical jurisprudence (law) or forensic medicine.
The seizing, confining, abducting, or carrying away of a person by force, including transporting a competent adult for medical treatment against his or her will.
questions.explanation: breach of confidentiality: Disclosure of information without proper authorization.

questions.question: Shortly before 7:00 a.m., a man was found lying facedown in a yard, cold, stiff, and pulseless. The responding paramedic testified the man was not breathing, had no pulse, and had obvious rigor mortis, and the court allowed that testimony as an observation a paramedic is trained to make when determining death. What does this case establish for EMTs?
choices: Resuscitation must be started on every pulseless patient, even when rigor mortis is clearly present.
EMTs are trained and expected to recognize rigor mortis as a definitive sign of death, to withhold resuscitation when it is present under protocol, and to document it plainly.
Only a physician or coroner may recognize or document signs of death at a scene.
A paramedic's observations of a body at a scene are never admissible in court proceedings.
questions.explanation: Recognizing postmortem muscle stiffening as a sign of death is squarely within EMT training and practice.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: The communication of false information about a person that is damaging to that person's reputation or standing in the community.
choices: defamation
contributory negligence
false imprisonment
competent
questions.explanation: defamation: The communication of false information about a person that is damaging to that person's reputation or standing in the community.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: Unilateral termination of care by the EMT without the patient's consent and without making provisions for continuing care by a medical professional who is training at the same level or higher.
choices: abandonment
forcible restraint
expressed consent
slander
questions.explanation: abandonment: Unilateral termination of care by the EMT without the patient's consent and without making provisions for continuing care by a medical professional who is training at the same level or higher.

questions.question: What does the term "protected health information" mean?
choices: A term relating to medical jurisprudence (law) or forensic medicine.
Failure to provide the same care that a person with similar training would provide.
Any information about health status, provision of health care, or payment for health care that can be linked to an individual.
The philosophy of right and wrong, of moral duties, and of ideal professional behavior.
questions.explanation: protected health information: Any information about health status, provision of health care, or payment for health care that can be linked to an individual.

questions.question: YOU are the Provider (32-year-old man, severe headache): Does HIPAA affect the medical care you provide to your patients? What information are you allowed to discuss with family members, bystanders, the media, and others?
choices: HIPAA allows you to discuss the patient's condition with family members and bystanders who were present, but prohibits telling the receiving hospital anything beyond the chief complaint.
HIPAA requires you to give the media a general statement about the patient's condition, as long as you do not use the patient's full name.
HIPAA limits the care you can provide, because you may not perform any assessment or treatment until the patient signs a HIPAA privacy notice at the scene.

HIPAA does not affect the medical care you provide, but it affects what information you can disclose. You may discuss the patient's condition with those involved in his care, such as other health care providers, but must not disclose information to family members, bystanders, or the media without the patient's consent, except as allowed by law.
questions.explanation: From the book's printed YOU are the Provider summary.

questions.question: Your partner, frustrated with a screaming patient, says, 'Keep it up and I'll sedate you until you can't talk.' The patient goes silent in fear. How should this be classified?
choices: false imprisonment
battery
gross negligence
assault
questions.explanation: Threatening a medical intervention as punishment unlawfully places the patient in fear of bodily harm, which meets the definition of assault.

questions.question: A patient claims an ambulance call report defamed her because it noted her anxiety, yelling, and aggressiveness and that she sometimes becomes violent. The court finds the report was not published to outsiders and was not defamatory because it recorded the paramedic's good-faith observations of her behavior on the call. What charting practice does this case support?
choices: Chart only what you observe, in neutral behavioral terms; a factual, good-faith run report is the best defense against a defamation claim.
Read the finished report to bystanders at the scene to confirm its accuracy before submitting it.
Leave all patient behavior out of the run report so it can never be used against the agency.
Include conclusions about the patient's character so readers understand what the crew dealt with.
questions.explanation: Chart only what you observe, in neutral behavioral terms; a factual, good-faith run report is the best defense against a defamation claim.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: Ability to understand and process information and make a choice regarding appropriate medical care.
choices: HIPAA
battery
negligence
decision-making capacity
questions.explanation: decision-making capacity: Ability to understand and process information and make a choice regarding appropriate medical care.

questions.question: What does the term "algor mortis" mean?
choices: Cooling of the body after death until it matches the ambient temperature.
The written or electronic legal record of an EMS call, which courts treat as a reflection of the care itself, so that an incomplete or untidy report is read as evidence of inadequate care.
The study of ethics related to issues that arise in health care.
Permission for treatment given by a competent patient after the potential risks, benefits, and alternatives to treatment have been explained.
questions.explanation: algor mortis: Cooling of the body after death until it matches the ambient temperature.

questions.question: An unconscious trauma patient with a crushed, bleeding leg needs a tourniquet and transport, but her parents cannot be reached. What allows you to treat and transport her?
choices: court-ordered consent
parental consent
implied consent
expressed consent
questions.explanation: In an emergency where the patient cannot consent and no surrogate is available, the law assumes she would want treatment.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: When the EMT or an EMS system is held liable even when the plaintiff is unable to clearly demonstrate how an injury occurred.
choices: res ipsa loquitur
chain of evidence
patient autonomy
duty to act
questions.explanation: res ipsa loquitur: When the EMT or an EMS system is held liable even when the plaintiff is unable to clearly demonstrate how an injury occurred.

questions.question: A researcher receives a data set of 500 transports with ages and zip codes but no names, addresses, or any way to link records to a person. Why is this set generally not treated as PHI?
choices: the data came from a public hospital
the records are more than one year old
it cannot be linked to an individual
the researcher signed a confidentiality agreement
questions.explanation: PHI must be linkable to an individual; properly de-identified data with no link back falls outside the definition.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: Stiffening of the body muscles; a definitive sign of death.
choices: breach of confidentiality
rigor mortis
putrefaction
morality
questions.explanation: rigor mortis: Stiffening of the body muscles; a definitive sign of death.

questions.question: A health care district's trauma agency director wrote a letter to a certifying group stating that a paramedic training company had billed the district for a course the district could not confirm took place, implying fraud and asking for an investigation. The company was suspended from hosting courses, an investigation found no billing impropriety, and a jury later awarded the company $692,400 for defamation. What is the lesson for EMS providers?
choices: A written accusation is protected as long as it also requests an investigation.
Never put an unproven accusation of fraud or misconduct in a letter, email, or report, because in writing it is preserved, forwarded, and sued over.
A letter sent between agencies can never be the basis of a libel suit.
Defamation claims can only arise from spoken statements, never from letters.
questions.explanation: A single written letter containing a false, damaging claim of fraud produced a six-figure defamation verdict.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: The principle of law that permits a health care provider to treat a patient in an emergency situation when the patient is incapable of granting consent because of an altered level of consciousness, disability, the effects of drugs or alcohol, or the patient's age.
choices: health care directive
emergency
rigor mortis
emergency doctrine
questions.explanation: emergency doctrine: The principle of law that permits a health care provider to treat a patient in an emergency situation when the patient is incapable of granting consent because of an altered level of consciousness, disability, the effects of drugs or alcohol, or the patient's age.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: Most commonly defined by state law; outlines the care that the EMT is able to provide for the patient.
choices: scope of practice
rigor mortis
interrogatories
chain of evidence
questions.explanation: scope of practice: Most commonly defined by state law; outlines the care that the EMT is able to provide for the patient.

questions.question: What does the term "statute of limitations" mean?
choices: Decomposition of body tissues; a definitive sign of death.
The time within which a legal case must be commenced.
Cooling of the body after death until it matches the ambient temperature.
Unilateral termination of care by the EMT without the patient's consent and without making provisions for continuing care by a medical professional who is training at the same level or higher.
questions.explanation: statute of limitations: The time within which a legal case must be commenced.

questions.question: An attorney explains that neither side wants surprises at trial, so each side will depose the other's witnesses and exchange expert reports over the next four months. What is this process called?
choices: voir dire
mediation
discovery
the arraignment process
questions.explanation: Exchanging information and taking depositions so both sides can build and evaluate their cases is discovery.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: Unlawfully touching a patient or providing emergency care without consent.
choices: patient autonomy
battery
HIPAA
assault
questions.explanation: battery: Unlawfully touching a patient or providing emergency care without consent.

questions.question: What does the term "depositions" mean?
choices: Refers to the legal responsibility of a person or organization to take on some of the functions and responsibilities of a parent.
Oral questions asked of parties and witnesses under oath.
Cooling of the body after death until it matches the ambient temperature.
The act of physically preventing an individual from initiating any physical action.
questions.explanation: depositions: Oral questions asked of parties and witnesses under oath.

questions.question: After a wrongful-death verdict, a jury awards a family money for lost future earnings and loss of companionship, with no amount meant to punish the agency. These awards are best classified as what?
choices: punitive damages
exemplary damages
liquidated damages
compensatory damages
questions.explanation: Awards that compensate for actual economic and noneconomic loss, rather than punish, are compensatory damages.

questions.question: Georgette Malette arrived unconscious after a severe 1979 car crash carrying a signed Jehovah's Witness card refusing blood transfusion under any circumstances; her doctor transfused her anyway to save her life, and a Canadian court awarded her $20,000 for battery. What should an EMT do with this lesson on scene?
choices: Rely on implied consent, which overrides any written refusal while the patient is unconscious.
Proceed with life-saving treatment, because a provider's good intention excuses treating over a refusal.
Check for wallet cards, directives, and medical alerts before treating an unconscious patient — a known refusal binds you even in an emergency.
Treat first in every emergency, because a wallet card has no legal effect on the care you provide.
questions.explanation: Malette v. Shulman held that transfusing against a known refusal is battery — life-saving intent does not excuse the unlawful touching.

questions.question: What does the term "do not resuscitate order" mean?
choices: The legal duty of an EMT to notify the appropriate authorities in specific situations, such as suspected child or elder abuse or neglect, injuries caused by weapons or crimes, and attempted suicide.
Written documentation by a physician giving permission to medical personnel not to attempt resuscitation in the event of cardiac arrest.
The right of a patient to make informed choices regarding his or her health care.
A legal defense that may be raised when the defendant thinks that the conduct of the plaintiff somehow contributed to any injuries or damages that were sustained by the plaintiff.
questions.explanation: do not resuscitate order: Written documentation by a physician giving permission to medical personnel not to attempt resuscitation in the event of cardiac arrest.

questions.question: What does the term "consent" mean?
choices: Stiffening of the body muscles; a definitive sign of death.
Permission to render care.
The written or electronic legal record of an EMS call, which courts treat as a reflection of the care itself, so that an incomplete or untidy report is read as evidence of inadequate care.
Unlawfully placing a patient in fear of bodily harm.
questions.explanation: consent: Permission to render care.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: The phase of a civil lawsuit where the plaintiff and defense obtain information from each other that will help both build their cases.
choices: discovery
emergency
morality
medicolegal
questions.explanation: discovery: The phase of a civil lawsuit where the plaintiff and defense obtain information from each other that will help both build their cases.

questions.question: A caller reports a terrible smell from a vacant house for two weeks. Inside, crews find a deceased person whose tissues are breaking down and liquefying. What is this process called?
choices: putrefaction
rigor mortis
postmortem cooling
dependent lividity
questions.explanation: The breakdown and decomposition of body tissues after death is putrefaction.

questions.question: An EMT knowingly leaves a patient in clear respiratory distress unattended for nearly 20 minutes without checking airway, breathing, or vital signs, because officers are still talking to him. What level of negligence is this inaction most likely to be called?
choices: res ipsa loquitur
gross negligence
ordinary negligence
negligence per se
questions.explanation: Doing nothing at all for a distressed patient you have a duty to assess is a reckless disregard of that duty.

questions.question: A jury awards a patient money for his actual medical bills, then adds a second, larger amount because the defendant's conduct was intentional and showed a willful and wanton disregard for public safety. What is the second amount called?
choices: incidental damages
punitive damages
compensatory damages
general damages
questions.explanation: The definition fits exactly: damages awarded when conduct was intentional or a willful and wanton disregard for the safety of the public and the rights of others.

questions.question: During a mass-casualty incident, a crew leader assigns the only ventilator to the patient most likely to survive instead of the first patient found. Which concept describes using ethical principles to make this professional decision?
choices: protocol compliance
standard of care
incident command
applied ethics
questions.explanation: Triage decision-making applies ethical principles such as justice and beneficence in real professional practice.

questions.question: An EMT attempted to resuscitate a 66-year-old woman in cardiac arrest, and the family later alleged he intubated her esophagus instead of her trachea, causing her death. The appellate court decided the case largely on the facts the EMT gave under oath before trial, describing how he prepared the patient and visualized the airway. What is the key lesson about that sworn testimony?
choices: Deposition answers can be corrected freely at trial if they conflict with the run report.
A deposition is informal, so minor differences from the run report carry no weight.
Your deposition will be compared line by line with your run report; the two must match.
Only the medical director's testimony is compared against the run report, not the EMT's.
questions.explanation: Deposition testimony is sworn evidence, and any conflict with the run report undermines the provider's credibility.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: Failure to provide the same care that a person with similar training would provide.
choices: patient autonomy
negligence
battery
assault
questions.explanation: negligence: Failure to provide the same care that a person with similar training would provide.

questions.question: A coworker who was not on your call asks you to pull up the electronic report of a well-known local athlete you transported so he can see what happened. You refuse because he has no role in the patient's care. Which federal law are you following?
choices: HIPAA
EMTALA
The OSHA bloodborne pathogens standard
The Stark Law
questions.explanation: HIPAA limits use and disclosure of protected health information to those with a legitimate need related to care, payment, or operations.

questions.question: Two years after a difficult airway call, an EMT is ordered to appear at a law office, is sworn in by a court reporter, and answers oral questions from the plaintiff's attorney while a transcript is made. What is this proceeding called?
choices: interrogatory
a preliminary hearing
grand jury testimony
deposition
questions.explanation: A deposition is oral questioning of a party or witness under oath during discovery.

questions.question: A homeless man's DNA was found under the fingernails of a home-invasion murder victim, and he was charged with murder and jailed for about five months. Hospital records then proved he had been in a hospital bed at the time of the killing; investigators concluded the same paramedics had treated him hours earlier and that a pulse oximeter clipped to both men's fingers had likely transferred his DNA to the victim. What lesson does this hold for EMTs?
choices: DNA found at a scene always proves the person was physically present there.
Paramedics should refuse to treat a second patient on the same shift to prevent any transfer.
Reusable equipment only needs cleaning when it is visibly soiled with blood.
EMTs must clean or replace equipment between patients and be aware that their own movements can transfer evidence into or out of a scene.
questions.explanation: EMS equipment carried one patient's DNA onto a victim, creating physical evidence that pointed at an innocent man.

questions.question: A competent adult with chest pain listens to your explanation and says, 'No IV, no monitor, and I am not going to the hospital.' Forcing treatment anyway would violate which requirement?
choices: scope of practice
duty to act
consent
confidentiality
questions.explanation: Care requires the patient's permission; a competent patient's refusal withdraws that permission.

questions.question: What does the term "libel" mean?
choices: The time within which a legal case must be commenced.
False and damaging information about a person that is communicated in writing.
Permission to render care.
The manner in which principles of ethics are incorporated into professional conduct.
questions.explanation: libel: False and damaging information about a person that is communicated in writing.

questions.question: An EMT wants to override a patient's refusal because the patient chose the option the crew considers unwise. The patient is oriented, understands the risks, and gives consistent reasons. What is the patient's status?
choices: incompetent
treated under implied consent
competent
mentally incapacitated
questions.explanation: Competence is the ability to make rational decisions about personal well-being, not agreement with the provider's recommendation.

questions.question: A 21-year-old woman is left in a persistent vegetative state and placed on a ventilator. She left no written instructions about her treatment wishes. Her parents ask that the ventilator be removed, but her doctors and the hospital refuse, and a court ultimately has to decide who can state her wishes for her. What should this case teach an EMT to do on calls involving incapacitated patients?
choices: Ask early about an advance directive or living will on every incapacitated patient, and document and relay whatever the family produces.
Accept a relative's verbal account as legally equal to a signed written directive.
Tell the family the crew can decide whether life support continues when no document exists.
Refuse to transport the patient until a court order settles the family's dispute.
questions.explanation: With no written directive, a court had to decide who could state the patient's wishes — the gap an advance directive is meant to fill.

questions.question: An EMT is ordered by a supervisor to falsify a run report's response time. She refuses because her personal and professional code of right and wrong will not let her lie on a patient record. What concept is guiding her refusal?
choices: scope of practice
ethics board policy
morality
statutory duty
questions.explanation: Morality is the code of conduct, defined by society, religion, or the person, that affects character, conduct, and conscience.

questions.question: A competent 28-year-old with quadriplegia and severe cerebral palsy is being fed through a nasogastric tube inserted against her will, and she clearly demands its removal. She fully understands her condition and the effect of removing the tube. What should govern her care?
choices: Her disability means she lacks capacity, so the treatment team should decide for her.
Her refusal is valid only if her family agrees with it.
Her refusal should be respected, because severe physical disability does not remove decision-making capacity when the patient can understand and process the choice.
A request to remove life-sustaining feeding is automatically invalid and can be ignored.
questions.explanation: Never equate disability, age, or diagnosis with incapacity; test understanding, not appearance.

questions.question: What does the term "patient care documentation" mean?
choices: The written or electronic legal record of an EMS call, which courts treat as a reflection of the care itself, so that an incomplete or untidy report is read as evidence of inadequate care.
Stiffening of the body muscles; a definitive sign of death.
The confinement of a person without legal authority or the person's consent.
A written document that specifies medical treatment for a competent patient, should he or she become unable to make decisions in the future; also known as an advance directive or a living will.
questions.explanation: patient care documentation: The written or electronic legal record of an EMS call, which courts treat as a reflection of the care itself, so that an incomplete or untidy report is read as evidence of inadequate care.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: False and damaging information about a person that is communicated in writing.
choices: emergency doctrine
libel
slander
torts
questions.explanation: libel: False and damaging information about a person that is communicated in writing.

questions.question: What does the term "governmental immunity" mean?
choices: Written, accepted levels of emergency care expected by reason of training and profession; written by legal or professional organizations so that patients are not exposed to unreasonable risk or harm.
Disclosure of information without proper authorization.
Written questions that the defense and plaintiff send to one another.

Legal doctrine that can protect an EMS provider from being sued or that may limit the amount of the monetary judgement (the amount of money that a court of law orders one person to pay to another) against the EMS provider.
questions.explanation: governmental immunity: Legal doctrine that can protect an EMS provider from being sued or that may limit the amount of the monetary judgement (the amount of money that a court of law orders one person to pay to another) against the EMS provider.

questions.question: A family sued a city after its EMTs allegedly failed and refused to provide emergency care to a 25-year-old pregnant woman having difficulty breathing at her cashier job. In the civil case, both sides exchanged interrogatories and document production, and deposed witnesses including the FDNY EMS chief. What should EMTs take from how this case was litigated?
choices: Discovery is limited to the patient care report and cannot reach recordings.
Depositions are voluntary, and a provider may decline to answer questions.
Everything discovery can reach, including dispatch recordings, protocols, and your own statements, is created on the day of the call, so document as if a deposition is coming.
Statements a provider made before the lawsuit was filed are exempt from discovery.
questions.explanation: Document every call as if a deposition is coming, because discovery can reach it all.

questions.question: A sedated patient arrives at the hospital with a dislocated shoulder that was not present before transport, and no one can explain how it happened during loading. The family sues, arguing the injury itself proves carelessness. Which doctrine are they invoking?
choices: proximate cause
res ipsa loquitur
gross negligence
implied consent
questions.explanation: Res ipsa loquitur holds the provider liable even when the plaintiff cannot clearly demonstrate how the injury occurred, because the injury ordinarily does not happen without negligence.

questions.question: After surgery, imaging shows a surgical sponge left inside the patient. The patient cannot identify which team member miscounted. Under which doctrine may the jury infer negligence from the retained sponge alone?
choices: assumption of risk
res ipsa loquitur
informed consent
strict liability
questions.explanation: A retained foreign object is the classic res ipsa case: the thing speaks for itself and the plaintiff need not prove the exact negligent act.

questions.question: Assessment in Action: What is the best way to care for your patient once he tells you he does not want to go to the hospital?
choices: Let him know how important it is that he accept transport to the hospital.
Ask him to sign a refusal form, releasing you from liability.
Order him to go to the hospital against his wishes.
Encourage him to call 9-1-1 again if his condition worsens.
questions.explanation: From the book's printed answer key.

questions.question: What does the term "contributory negligence" mean?
choices: Statutory provisions enacted by many states to protect citizens from liability for errors and omissions in giving good faith emergency medical care, unless there is wanton, gross, or willful negligence.

Legal doctrine that can protect an EMS provider from being sued or that may limit the amount of the monetary judgement (the amount of money that a court of law orders one person to pay to another) against the EMS provider.
Oral questions asked of parties and witnesses under oath.
A legal defense that may be raised when the defendant thinks that the conduct of the plaintiff somehow contributed to any injuries or damages that were sustained by the plaintiff.
