questions.explanation: contributory negligence: A legal defense that may be raised when the defendant thinks that the conduct of the plaintiff somehow contributed to any injuries or damages that were sustained by the plaintiff.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: The written or electronic legal record of an EMS call, which courts treat as a reflection of the care itself, so that an incomplete or untidy report is read as evidence of inadequate care.
choices: ethics
health care directive
emergency medical care
patient care documentation
questions.explanation: patient care documentation: The written or electronic legal record of an EMS call, which courts treat as a reflection of the care itself, so that an incomplete or untidy report is read as evidence of inadequate care.

questions.question: A patient executed a durable power of attorney for health care last year while fully competent. She is now comatose. When does her agent's authority to make treatment decisions operate?
choices: only after a court declares her incompetent
only during the final days of a terminal illness
immediately upon signing the document
when she is unable to make decisions herself
questions.explanation: By definition the appointed agent acts on the patient's behalf when the patient is unable to do so.
questions.topic: durable power of attorney for health care

questions.question: A paramedic places an IV medication at ten times the protocol dose because she never checked the drug reference every other medic in her system uses, and the patient is harmed. Which term describes her care?
choices: false imprisonment
assault
abandonment
negligence
questions.explanation: Her care fell below what a person with similar training would provide in the same situation, which is the definition of negligence.

questions.question: In a federal civil lawsuit over a man's death three days after a police beating, the parties spent years filing motions about depositions, with the plaintiff seeking to expand depositions from 30 to 44. The city reported the plaintiff had requested over 8,000 body-worn camera videos and over a million pages of documents and had taken 31 depositions, including of fire department personnel. What does the scale of this case show?
choices: Discovery in a high-profile case can run for years and cover every video and page, so there is no such thing as an off-the-record run report.
Video recordings are exempt from discovery because they are police property.
Only police officers, not EMTs, can be deposed in a civil lawsuit.
Discovery normally wraps up within a few weeks of the lawsuit being filed.
questions.explanation: Discovery can run for years and cover every video and page in a major case.

questions.question: A man suffered a stroke while driving and drifted onto a sidewalk. Responders mistook him for intoxicated, the first ambulance left without him, and his treatment was delayed. He sued only for the worsening caused by the delay, and the defense argued that his failure to control his high blood pressure made him partly at fault for his own outcome. What does this case illustrate about that defense?
choices: Crews cannot blame a patient for causing the emergency they were called to treat; liability turns on the care given after arrival.
The patient's pre-existing condition transfers all liability to his personal physician.
A patient who contributes to his own emergency automatically loses the right to recover any damages.
A delayed response is never negligent when the patient's own condition caused the call.
questions.explanation: Conduct that merely triggers the need for aid cannot be used as a contributory negligence defense; the care after arrival is what counts.

questions.question: What does the term "abandonment" mean?
choices: The federal law, enacted in 1996, that protects the privacy and security of a patient's health information and limits how EMS personnel may use or share it.
Unilateral termination of care by the EMT without the patient's consent and without making provisions for continuing care by a medical professional who is training at the same level or higher.
The seizing, confining, abducting, or carrying away of a person by force, including transporting a competent adult for medical treatment against his or her will.
Refers to the legal responsibility of a person or organization to take on some of the functions and responsibilities of a parent.
questions.explanation: abandonment: Unilateral termination of care by the EMT without the patient's consent and without making provisions for continuing care by a medical professional who is training at the same level or higher.

questions.question: Two bombs explode near the finish line of the Boston Marathon in 2013, killing 3 spectators and wounding more than 260 people, many with traumatic amputations. Medical tent volunteers and EMS crews provide rapid tourniquet use and fast transport, and no one who reached a hospital alive died. In a blast or mass-shooting emergency like this one, what comes first?
choices: Immediate hemorrhage control comes before almost everything else in the primary assessment.
A complete secondary assessment should be finished before any bleeding is treated.
Every patient should be formally triaged and tagged before any tourniquets are applied.
Crews should wait for additional units to arrive before beginning treatment of the wounded.
questions.explanation: In blast and mass-shooting emergencies, immediate hemorrhage control comes before almost everything else in the primary assessment.

questions.question: In 1959, four-month-old Darien Manlove, with diarrhea and a fever above 102 degrees, was brought to a hospital emergency ward; the nurse did not examine him or take his temperature and turned the family away because the child was under private doctors' care, and he died that afternoon of bronchial pneumonia. What duty does this case place on emergency providers?
choices: Emergency departments may screen incoming patients by whether the family already has a physician.
Never turn a patient away unexamined; if a presentation could be an emergency, assess first and let a physician decide.
A patient who is under a private doctor's care can safely be sent away without an examination.
A nurse may decline to assess an infant whose symptoms appear minor at the front desk.
questions.explanation: Manlove held that a hospital holding out emergency services may be liable for refusing treatment in an unmistakable emergency.

questions.question: Your crew finds an unresponsive patient in a nursing home. Staff hand you a signed living will stating the patient refused artificial nutrition and hydration if in a persistent vegetative state. How should this document be treated?
choices: an expired document once the patient enters a nursing home
a suggestion only, which the crew may disregard if the family objects
health care directive (honor it and verify it under local protocol)
a hospital-only form that EMS is not permitted to follow
questions.explanation: The living will is a health care directive: the patient's own written treatment instructions, made while competent, for exactly this situation.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: Written, accepted levels of emergency care expected by reason of training and profession; written by legal or professional organizations so that patients are not exposed to unreasonable risk or harm.
choices: in loco parentis
proximate causation
duty to act
standard of care
questions.explanation: standard of care: Written, accepted levels of emergency care expected by reason of training and profession; written by legal or professional organizations so that patients are not exposed to unreasonable risk or harm.

questions.question: City 911 dispatchers twice refused to send an ambulance to a woman in labor. She was seriously injured in a car crash while being driven to the hospital, and her baby died after delivery. She sued the city for negligence, but the state supreme court ruled against her. Why did the claim fail?
choices: The claim failed because the woman did not suffer any actual damages.
The claim failed because dispatchers owe no duty to callers requesting an ambulance.
The claim failed because governmental agencies cannot be sued for negligence.
Even with a duty and a breach, the claim failed on proximate causation: the city's conduct was not a proximate cause of her injuries.
questions.explanation: Causation is a separate element of negligence that the plaintiff must prove, apart from duty and breach.

questions.question: An on-duty EMT crew is dispatched to a chest pain call in their district. The crew considers clearing as 'probably nothing.' What legal concept requires them to respond and provide care?
choices: standard of care
scope of practice
duty to act
Good Samaritan protection
questions.explanation: By statute and by their function as on-duty responders, they have a responsibility to provide care.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: Any information about health status, provision of health care, or payment for health care that can be linked to an individual.
choices: battery
ethics
advance directive
protected health information
questions.explanation: protected health information: Any information about health status, provision of health care, or payment for health care that can be linked to an individual.

questions.question: A summer camp counselor signs a permission form for a camper's stitches while the parents are on a flight and unreachable. The camp is exercising what legal responsibility?
choices: substituted judgment
in loco parentis
expressed consent
temporary guardianship
questions.explanation: The organization temporarily standing in the place of a parent acts in loco parentis.

questions.question: Which responder is acting outside the usual scope of Good Samaritan protection?
choices: Good Samaritan laws (a provider giving care for payment / in a hospital as part of regular duties)
Good Samaritan laws (a volunteer first responder helping at a community event)
Good Samaritan laws (a bystander who holds pressure on a bleeding wound)
Good Samaritan laws (an off-duty EMT who stops at a roadside crash)
questions.explanation: Good Samaritan statutes protect unpaid, good faith emergency help, not care given for compensation or as part of regular in-hospital duties.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: Damages awarded in a civil lawsuit that are intended to restore the plaintiff to the same condition that he or she was in prior to the incident complained about in the lawsuit.
choices: bioethics
chain of evidence
algor mortis
compensatory damages
questions.explanation: compensatory damages: Damages awarded in a civil lawsuit that are intended to restore the plaintiff to the same condition that he or she was in prior to the incident complained about in the lawsuit.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: The documented, unbroken record of everyone who collected, handled, and transferred physical evidence from a crime scene, maintained so the evidence stays usable in court.
choices: consent
patient care documentation
chain of evidence
Good Samaritan laws
questions.explanation: chain of evidence: The documented, unbroken record of everyone who collected, handled, and transferred physical evidence from a crime scene, maintained so the evidence stays usable in court.

questions.question: Which of the following items from a patient care report is protected health information?
choices: protected health information (the patient's name linked to her diagnosis and treatment)
the patient's age and zip code with no other details attached
a list of diagnoses with no names or identifiers attached to it
the total number of transports your agency ran that month
questions.explanation: A name linked to health status or care provided can be tied to an individual, which is the definition of protected health information.

questions.question: Your medical director asks why a new EMT must follow the system's written protocols instead of improvising care he saw online. The best answer is that protocols reflect what?
choices: implied consent
standard of care
certification requirements
medical control
questions.explanation: Protocols state the written, accepted level of care for the profession, written so patients are not exposed to unreasonable risk or harm.

questions.question: What does the term "gross negligence" mean?
choices: Conduct that constitutes a willful or reckless disregard for a duty or standard of care.
Any information about health status, provision of health care, or payment for health care that can be linked to an individual.
False and damaging information about a person that is communicated in writing.
The seizing, confining, abducting, or carrying away of a person by force, including transporting a competent adult for medical treatment against his or her will.
questions.explanation: gross negligence: Conduct that constitutes a willful or reckless disregard for a duty or standard of care.

questions.question: What does the term "applied ethics" mean?
choices: The time within which a legal case must be commenced.
The federal law, enacted in 1996, that protects the privacy and security of a patient's health information and limits how EMS personnel may use or share it.
A type of consent in which a patient gives verbal or nonverbal authorization for provision of care or transport.
The manner in which principles of ethics are incorporated into professional conduct.
questions.explanation: applied ethics: The manner in which principles of ethics are incorporated into professional conduct.

questions.question: A patient with a psychological disorder repeatedly tried to leave a moving ambulance, unbuckled her stretcher belts, and said she would jump. The paramedics used talk-down techniques but did not physically restrain her; she opened the rear door, jumped, and died. A jury found for the family, and the appeals court rejected the agency's argument on proximate cause. What does this case teach?
choices: Proximate cause can never be based on something a provider failed to do.
Foreseeable patient behavior creates a duty to act; failing to restrain a patient who announces she will jump can be the proximate cause of her death.
A patient's own decision to jump always breaks the chain of causation for the crew.
Talk-down techniques alone satisfy the duty of care for a patient threatening to jump.
questions.explanation: The court treated the failure to restrain as a proximate cause because the harm was foreseeable and flowed directly from the breach.

questions.question: A 15-year-old boy is run over by a train car, crushing and mangling his left foot. Five physicians agree immediate amputation is necessary to save his life. The boy is unconscious and no parent or relative is available to consent, so the surgeons amputate without it, and the Michigan Supreme Court upholds a verdict for the doctors. What should an EMT take from this case?
choices: Consent is unnecessary for any procedure once an emergency patient reaches a hospital.
The crew should delay treatment until law enforcement locates a family member to sign consent forms.
In a life-threatening emergency with an incapacitated patient and no surrogate available, treat the patient and document the emergency and your attempts to reach family.
A minor must never be treated without a parent's consent, even when delay would likely be fatal.
questions.explanation: In a life-threatening emergency with an incapacitated patient and no surrogate available, treat and document the emergency and your attempts to reach family.

questions.question: A paramedic gives only a truncated evaluation to a man during a police encounter, missing what a full assessment would have found; the man dies, and a court later calls the brief evaluation an extreme departure from accepted care. What does this case teach the EMT?
choices: A brief visual check is sufficient whenever another agency controls the patient.
Defer to police custody decisions and limit your exam to what officers request.
Do a complete assessment even when police are in charge of the person; a brief look is not the standard of care.
Keep documentation short; detailed assessments are only required during transport.
questions.explanation: A complete assessment is owed even when police control the person; a truncated evaluation breaches the standard of care.

questions.question: What does the term "mandatory reporting" mean?
choices: The legal duty of an EMT to notify the appropriate authorities in specific situations, such as suspected child or elder abuse or neglect, injuries caused by weapons or crimes, and attempted suicide.
Wrongful acts that give rise to a civil lawsuit.

Statutory provisions enacted by many states to protect citizens from liability for errors and omissions in giving good faith emergency medical care, unless there is wanton, gross, or willful negligence.
The federal law, enacted in 1996, that protects the privacy and security of a patient's health information and limits how EMS personnel may use or share it.
questions.explanation: mandatory reporting: The legal duty of an EMT to notify the appropriate authorities in specific situations, such as suspected child or elder abuse or neglect, injuries caused by weapons or crimes, and attempted suicide.

questions.question: A patient agrees to an examination under anesthesia but expressly refuses surgery if a tumor is found; surgeons remove a fibroid tumor anyway while she is asleep. What rule does this classic case establish for the EMT?
choices: Consent for an examination covers related procedures the team judges necessary.
Consent to one procedure is not consent to another; honor the limits a competent patient sets.
Family consent obtained afterward can validate treatment already given.
Once a patient is under anesthesia, the team may treat anything it finds.
questions.explanation: A competent patient's consent has limits, and treatment beyond them violates the patient's right to decide.

questions.question: Navigate Case Study (32-year-old man, low blood glucose): If you had left the scene as the patient requested, what would you and your partner be accused of?
choices: Battery, because leaving the scene after arriving at the patient's home would be treated the same as unwanted physical contact with the patient.

Abandonment. Leaving a patient who still needs care without transferring him to someone of equal or higher medical training can be abandonment and negligence, and his request would not protect you because his confusion meant he was not competent to refuse.
False imprisonment, because remaining responsible for a patient after he has been found is the same as holding him against his will.
Nothing, because a patient who tells the crew to leave has formally refused care, and honoring that request protects the crew from any accusation.
questions.explanation: Answer written from the chapter (no printed key).

questions.question: Which of the following is the best example of an emergency as defined in your textbook?
choices: emergency — a patient with a minor ankle sprain who is able to walk to the ambulance
emergency — a stable patient requesting transport for a scheduled dialysis appointment
emergency — a nursing home resident with a chronic cough that has not changed
emergency — a patient with an obstructed airway who is turning cyanotic
questions.explanation: An obstructed airway is a serious, life-threatening situation requiring immediate intervention; routine transports and stable complaints are not.

questions.question: At a nursing home, staff hand you a signed state out-of-hospital DNR form for your pulseless, apneic patient and the form matches the patient. What should you do?
choices: do not resuscitate order
advance directive
health care power of attorney
living will
questions.explanation: A valid written physician DNR order directs medical personnel not to attempt resuscitation in cardiac arrest, so you withhold CPR and follow local protocol.

questions.question: In 1951, cells from a patient's cervical tumor were taken and cultured without her knowledge or consent, becoming the HeLa cell line used worldwide in research and commercial products. Her family learned of it decades later. What ethical duty was breached?
choices: Notifying the family decades later satisfies the duty to obtain consent.
A patient's body and information are not yours to use beyond the care they agreed to; consent and honesty are ethical duties, not paperwork.
No duty was breached, because tissue removed during treatment may be used freely for research.
Consent is required only when research is sold commercially, not for laboratory use.
questions.explanation: Using a patient's tissue without consent breached the moral duty to respect the patient as a person.

questions.question: What does the term "advance directive" mean?
choices: When a person who has a duty abuses it, and causes harm to another individual, the EMT, the agency, and/or the medical director may be sued for negligence.
False and damaging information about a person that is communicated in writing.
False and damaging information about a person that is communicated by spoken word.
Written documentation that specifies medical treatment for a competent patient should the patient become unable to make decisions; also called a living will or a health care directive.
questions.explanation: advance directive: Written documentation that specifies medical treatment for a competent patient should the patient become unable to make decisions; also called a living will or a health care directive.

questions.question: Your ambulance service loses an unencrypted laptop containing 500 patient care reports, and federal regulators investigate the service's privacy and security practices. Which law gives those regulators their enforcement authority?
choices: The Federal Trade Commission Act
The Patient Safety and Quality Improvement Act
The Sarbanes-Oxley Act
HIPAA
questions.explanation: The HHS Office for Civil Rights enforces HIPAA's Privacy and Security Rules, including against ambulance services.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: Refers to the legal responsibility of a person or organization to take on some of the functions and responsibilities of a parent.
choices: in loco parentis
patient care documentation
gross negligence
libel
questions.explanation: in loco parentis: Refers to the legal responsibility of a person or organization to take on some of the functions and responsibilities of a parent.

questions.question: What does the term "emergency doctrine" mean?
choices: The study of ethics related to issues that arise in health care.
Written questions that the defense and plaintiff send to one another.
A person who is under the legal age in a given state but, because of other circumstances, is legally considered an adult.

The principle of law that permits a health care provider to treat a patient in an emergency situation when the patient is incapable of granting consent because of an altered level of consciousness, disability, the effects of drugs or alcohol, or the patient's age.
questions.explanation: emergency doctrine: The principle of law that permits a health care provider to treat a patient in an emergency situation when the patient is incapable of granting consent because of an altered level of consciousness, disability, the effects of drugs or alcohol, or the patient's age.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: A code of conduct that can be defined by society, religion, or a person, affecting character, conduct, and conscience.
choices: assault
morality
false imprisonment
standard of care
questions.explanation: morality: A code of conduct that can be defined by society, religion, or a person, affecting character, conduct, and conscience.

questions.question: A patient is injured during a transport in March 2023. State law gives two years to file a negligence suit. The patient first contacts the agency's risk manager in June 2025 asking how to sue. What legal concept will most likely decide whether the case can proceed?
choices: res ipsa loquitur
statute of limitations
contributory negligence
sovereign immunity
questions.explanation: The statute of limitations is the time within which a legal case must be commenced, and that two-year window has closed.

questions.question: A competent patient signs a transport consent form in the ambulance bay, but no one has told him anything about the treatment planned, its risks, or his alternatives. Why is this consent legally weak?
choices: the form was signed in the ambulance instead of at the hospital
informed consent was not obtained (permission without explanation of risks, benefits, and alternatives)
the signature was not witnessed by a second provider
consent forms are never valid for transport decisions
questions.explanation: Consent is only informed when the competent patient first receives an explanation of the potential risks, benefits, and alternatives.

questions.question: Navigate Case Study (32-year-old man, low blood glucose): You are dispatched to 2567 Walnut Lane for a confused male, unknown medical. Upon your arrival, you and your partner find a police officer attempting to calm a 32-year-old man who is somewhat confused and very agitated. When he sees you, he says he doesn’t want your help and asks you to leave immediately. You notice a box of syringes in the kitchen. What should you do now?
choices: Wait outside until a family member arrives to give consent, because a confused patient cannot be treated until a relative authorizes care.
Ask the police officer to arrest the patient so he can be transported, because EMS cannot legally assess or treat a patient who has told the crew to leave.

Do not leave. He is confused and agitated, so he lacks decision-making capacity and cannot refuse care; treat him under implied consent. Work with the police officer to keep the scene safe, assess for a medical cause of the confusion (the syringes suggest possible diabetes or drug use), check his blood glucose, and treat what you find.
Leave the scene as the patient requested, because any adult who verbally refuses care must be left alone, and document that the patient refused before you clear.
questions.explanation: Answer written from the chapter (no printed key).

questions.question: A competent patient with chest pain cannot speak comfortably, but when the EMT asks, 'May I put this oxygen mask on you?' the patient nods and leans forward so it can be placed. What type of consent is this?
choices: expressed consent
presumed consent
involuntary consent
implied consent
questions.explanation: A clear nonverbal authorization, a nod and cooperative movement in response to a direct question, is expressed consent.

questions.question: A patient's son demands you ignore his mother's signed directive refusing resuscitation attempts because 'she changed her mind last week,' but he has no documentation. What is the controlling document until medical direction rules otherwise?
choices: the most recent physician order written in the chart
the nursing home's standing care plan for the unit
health care directive
the son's verbal statement, as the closest living relative
questions.explanation: The signed health care directive is the patient's written specification of her treatment wishes; an undocumented verbal claim does not by itself replace it.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: The legal duty of an EMT to notify the appropriate authorities in specific situations, such as suspected child or elder abuse or neglect, injuries caused by weapons or crimes, and attempted suicide.
choices: mandatory reporting
dependent lividity
emergency
morality
questions.explanation: mandatory reporting: The legal duty of an EMT to notify the appropriate authorities in specific situations, such as suspected child or elder abuse or neglect, injuries caused by weapons or crimes, and attempted suicide.

questions.question: Which situation most clearly risks a false imprisonment claim? A) Transporting an unconscious trauma patient under implied consent B) Restraining a competent patient who has refused care and has decision-making capacity C) Transporting a patient on a valid involuntary psychiatric hold
choices: D) Restraining a violent patient who is actively endangering the crew
C) Transporting a patient on a valid involuntary psychiatric hold
B) Restraining a competent patient who has refused care and has decision-making capacity
A) Transporting an unconscious trauma patient under implied consent
questions.explanation: Only the competent refusing patient is being confined without consent or legal authority; the other two have legal justification.

questions.question: What does the term "res ipsa loquitur" mean?
choices: When the EMT or an EMS system is held liable even when the plaintiff is unable to clearly demonstrate how an injury occurred.
Any information about health status, provision of health care, or payment for health care that can be linked to an individual.
The legal duty of an EMT to notify the appropriate authorities in specific situations, such as suspected child or elder abuse or neglect, injuries caused by weapons or crimes, and attempted suicide.
The communication of false information about a person that is damaging to that person's reputation or standing in the community.
questions.explanation: res ipsa loquitur: When the EMT or an EMS system is held liable even when the plaintiff is unable to clearly demonstrate how an injury occurred.

questions.question: A judge explains that one part of a verdict repays the plaintiff's medical expenses and lost income, while a separate part punishes willful misconduct. The repayment part is what type of damages?
choices: punitive damages
compensatory damages
nominal damages
treble damages
questions.explanation: The portion intended to make the plaintiff whole for losses is compensatory; the punishment portion would be punitive damages.

questions.question: What does the term "implied consent" mean?
choices: A serious situation, such as injury or illness that threatens the life or welfare of a person or group of people and requires immediate intervention.
Wrongful acts that give rise to a civil lawsuit.
Type of consent in which a patient who is unable to give consent is given treatment under the legal assumption that he or she would want treatment.

Legal doctrine that can protect an EMS provider from being sued or that may limit the amount of the monetary judgement (the amount of money that a court of law orders one person to pay to another) against the EMS provider.
questions.explanation: implied consent: Type of consent in which a patient who is unable to give consent is given treatment under the legal assumption that he or she would want treatment.

questions.question: What does the term "defamation" mean?
choices: The seizing, confining, abducting, or carrying away of a person by force, including transporting a competent adult for medical treatment against his or her will.
Most commonly defined by state law; outlines the care that the EMT is able to provide for the patient.
The phase of a civil lawsuit where the plaintiff and defense obtain information from each other that will help both build their cases.
The communication of false information about a person that is damaging to that person's reputation or standing in the community.
questions.explanation: defamation: The communication of false information about a person that is damaging to that person's reputation or standing in the community.

questions.question: A 79-year-old woman spills coffee served at 180-190 degrees F in her lap, suffering third-degree burns that require eight days of hospitalization and skin grafting. The restaurant had refused her request of about $20,000, offering $800, and evidence showed it had received prior complaints about the coffee's temperature. A jury awards compensatory and punitive damages. What does this case show about tort suits?
choices: Punitive damages can never be awarded in a civil tort case.
Tort suits are criminal prosecutions that the state brings against a defendant.
Tort cases are civil: the remedy is money damages, and prior complaints and ignored warnings become key evidence.
Prior complaints about the same hazard are inadmissible in a tort case.
questions.explanation: The suit was a civil negligence/product tort over an allegedly wrongful act, not a criminal case.

questions.question: Between 2005 and 2008, employees at a large hospital repeatedly opened celebrity patients' electronic records with no treatment reason; one was indicted for selling information to a tabloid, 13 employees were fired, and the system paid $865,500 to settle the federal case. What does this case illustrate?
choices: Viewing a record is only a breach if the information is sold for money
Employees may view any record in their own facility as long as they do not print it
Celebrity records carry less protection because the patients are public figures
Curiosity is not authorization; only open records of patients you are actually treating.
questions.explanation: Accessing records without a job purpose is an unauthorized disclosure of confidential information, even when nothing is posted or sold.

questions.question: In Rochester, New York in 2020, Daniel Prude, 41, in a mental-health crisis, was handcuffed, hooded with a spit hood, and held face-down with his head pressed to the pavement for over two minutes until he stopped breathing; the medical examiner ruled his death a homicide from complications of asphyxia in the setting of physical restraint. What practice does his death demand of an EMT?
choices: Prone restraint is safe as long as the patient was still breathing at the moment he was handcuffed.
Placing a spit hood on a restrained patient removes the need to monitor that patient's breathing.
Never leave a restrained patient prone and unmonitored; the moment struggling stops may be the moment breathing stopped — reassess the airway immediately.
A restrained patient who stops struggling has calmed down and can safely be left prone for transport.
questions.explanation: Prude died of asphyxia during physical restraint — sudden quiet in a prone, restrained patient is a danger sign, not compliance.

questions.question: During CPR at a stabbing scene, you move a knife aside and later kick a shell casing without noticing. At trial, the defense argues the physical evidence cannot be trusted. What has your scene disturbance damaged?
choices: evidence-based practice
continuity of care
chain of command
chain of evidence
questions.explanation: Undocumented movement of evidence breaks the unbroken record needed for the evidence to stay usable in court.

questions.question: Assessment in Action: Upon arrival at the scene, your partner began assessing vital signs without talking to the patient. This demonstrates:
choices: effective interpersonal communication.
patient advocacy.
failure to obtain consent.
breach of duty.
questions.explanation: From the book's printed answer key.

questions.question: An off-duty EMT stops at a crash, holds pressure on a bleeding wound in good faith, and makes an honest error in care. A lawsuit follows. What most likely protects her?
choices: sovereign immunity
Good Samaritan laws
the standard of care
implied consent
questions.explanation: These statutes protect citizens from liability for errors and omissions in good faith emergency care, absent gross, wanton, or willful negligence.

questions.question: A 15-year-old is run over by a train car and arrives unconscious with a mangled, crushed foot. Five physicians agree immediate amputation is necessary to save his life, and no parent or relative can be reached. What should the surgeon do?
choices: Proceed with the life-saving treatment without parental consent, because the patient cannot consent and no surrogate is available, and document why consent could not be obtained.
Wait for the patient to regain consciousness so he can consent for himself.
Stabilize the boy but refuse any surgery until a court order is obtained.
Delay treatment until a parent or relative is located and can sign a consent form.
questions.explanation: When a patient cannot consent and no surrogate is reachable, treat the life threat and document why consent could not be obtained.

questions.question: Your patient dies en route after a stabbing, and the hospital asks you to document exactly where the knife was found, who handled it, and your times, for the police and the coroner. This documentation matters because the death is what?
choices: a routine natural death
outside the legal system
reportable only to the hospital
medicolegal
questions.explanation: Deaths from violence are medicolegal: they fall under medical jurisprudence and forensic investigation, so chain of custody and exact documentation are legally significant.

questions.question: Your partner suggests telling a frightened patient 'this won't hurt at all' about a procedure you know is painful, just to keep him calm. What professional issue is at stake?
choices: ethics
scope of practice
medical direction
standard of care
questions.explanation: Honesty with patients is a moral duty and part of ideal professional behavior, which is ethics.

questions.question: Your patient care report for a chest pain call is missing the second set of vital signs and has several blank fields. In the malpractice trial two years later, the plaintiff's attorney argues the missing entries prove the reassessment never happened. What legal record is he attacking?
choices: patient care documentation
quality improvement review
medical control authorization
incident report
questions.explanation: Courts treat the patient care report as a reflection of the care itself, so gaps are read as care that was not done.

questions.question: A forensic method estimates time of death from one rectal temperature, the ambient temperature, body weight, and corrective factors for clothing and surroundings; validated on 111 cases, its 95 percent confidence interval is plus or minus 2.8 hours for deaths within the first 10 hours. How should EMS treat this kind of estimate?
choices: Once a body feels cold, investigators no longer need temperature readings
A single rectal temperature can pinpoint the exact minute of death
Cooling gives a range, never an exact time; document scene temperature and do not disturb the body so investigators can use it.
Body cooling follows a fixed rate of exactly one degree per hour in all conditions
questions.explanation: The nomogram is algor mortis in practice, working backward from how far the body has cooled toward ambient temperature.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: Statutory provisions enacted by many states to protect citizens from liability for errors and omissions in giving good faith emergency medical care, unless there is wanton, gross, or willful negligence.
choices: proximate causation
applied ethics
emancipated minor
Good Samaritan laws
questions.explanation: Good Samaritan laws: Statutory provisions enacted by many states to protect citizens from liability for errors and omissions in giving good faith emergency medical care, unless there is wanton, gross, or willful negligence.

questions.question: YOU are the Provider (32-year-old man, severe headache): Are you legally authorized to treat this patient? Why or why not?
choices: No. EMTs are never authorized to treat a patient with a possible stroke until a physician at the hospital has granted permission by radio.
Yes. Because the call came through 9-1-1, the patient has already consented to assessment and treatment, so the crew may begin care without asking him.

No. He has not given consent. Although he is conscious and alert, you have not asked his permission to treat him. You must obtain consent before providing care, unless the patient is unconscious or otherwise unable to give consent.
Yes. A patient who is sitting in a public place and acknowledges the crew's presence has given implied consent to be assessed and treated.
questions.explanation: From the book's printed YOU are the Provider summary.

questions.question: A patient with an emotional crisis refuses transport. You tell him, 'Agree to go, or I'll have the police hold you down and strap you to the stretcher.' He becomes visibly frightened. What have you committed?
choices: assault
false imprisonment
negligence
battery
questions.explanation: Assault is unlawfully placing a patient in fear of bodily harm; threatening forced restraint to compel consent does this even without touching him.

questions.question: A patient consented to an examination under anesthesia but clearly said there must be no operation. While she was unconscious, the surgeon found a tumor and removed it anyway, with a good result. Why was the operation still a legal wrong?
choices: Implied consent allows providers to override a patient's stated refusal whenever they disagree with it.
Consent to an examination under anesthesia automatically includes consent to any surgery done during it.
Once a patient is unconscious, consent extends to any procedure the provider considers beneficial.
Implied consent covers only a true emergency when the patient cannot consent; it does not permit a non-emergency procedure the patient specifically refused.
questions.explanation: Implied consent covers only the emergency; a known refusal or a non-emergency procedure is not covered.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: A serious situation, such as injury or illness that threatens the life or welfare of a person or group of people and requires immediate intervention.
choices: patient autonomy
emergency
durable power of attorney for health care
gross negligence
questions.explanation: emergency: A serious situation, such as injury or illness that threatens the life or welfare of a person or group of people and requires immediate intervention.

questions.question: The estate of a patient sued a county EMS service for malpractice, alleging paramedics failed to give oxygen, gave too small a medication dose, and delayed transport with repeated intubation attempts. The court dismissed the case before trial, holding that ambulance service was a governmental function and the county's insurance policy did not waive its immunity. What does this case illustrate?
choices: A malpractice suit against a county EMS agency must always be decided by a jury.
Immunity protects a government agency only after its crew proves the care met the standard.
Governmental immunity can end a negligence suit against a government-run EMS agency before trial, regardless of whether the care provided was actually good.
Purchasing a liability insurance policy automatically waives a county's immunity.
questions.explanation: Immunity depends on who operates the service and on insurance wording, not on whether the care was good.

questions.question: A hospital patient with a valid DNR order arrests and a new nurse starts compressions before anyone checks the chart. Which document, had it been checked, gave permission not to attempt resuscitation?
choices: living will
do not resuscitate order
advance directive
durable power of attorney for health care
questions.explanation: The DNR order is the physician's written documentation telling personnel not to attempt resuscitation if arrest occurs.

questions.question: In 1977 a forensic anthropologist examined a relatively intact body in formal clothing from a disturbed Tennessee grave and estimated death within the past year — but the man was Colonel William Shy, killed in 1864, whose airtight cast-iron coffin and embalming had largely prevented decomposition for 113 years. What lesson does this hold for an EMT judging a body at a scene?
choices: A body with intact flesh and intestines remaining has been dead only a few months at most.
Putrefaction is a definitive sign of death when it is present, but decomposition does not run on a fixed clock — never estimate time of death in the field.
Crews should determine the time of death from tissue condition before calling the medical examiner.
An embalmed body in a sealed coffin will decompose at the same rate as any other body.
questions.explanation: Environment can dramatically slow or speed decomposition, so use putrefaction as a sign of death, never as a timeline.

questions.question: In Orlando in 2008, two-year-old Caylee Anthony was not reported missing for about 31 days; her grandmother told 911 the trunk of the mother's car smelled like a dead body, and the child's skeletal remains were later found in advanced decomposition. What does this case teach an EMT who finds a body in that condition?
choices: A body showing decomposition is definitively dead — do not start resuscitation, preserve the scene, and notify law enforcement and the medical examiner.
Begin CPR immediately, because a decomposition odor by itself never proves that death has occurred.
Move the remains somewhere cooler to slow decomposition before investigators arrive at the scene.
Estimate the time of death from the degree of decomposition and report your estimate to the family.
questions.explanation: Decomposition (putrefaction) is a definitive sign of death: withhold resuscitation, preserve the scene, and notify law enforcement and the medical examiner.

questions.question: A 92-year-old hospice patient with a living will refusing revival is found unresponsive. No DNR order was ever placed in her chart, so paramedics perform CPR, intubate her, and transport her; she dies days later after life support is removed. Why did EMS resuscitate?
choices: A living will alone is not an out-of-hospital DNR; without a signed order form EMS can see, resuscitation proceeds by default.
The physician's phone instruction to call 911 created a valid DNR order
The living will should have been treated by the paramedics as a valid DNR order
Enrollment in hospice care by itself legally functions as a DNR order
questions.explanation: Families and facilities must get the signed DNR order form where EMS can see it; a living will alone does not authorize withholding resuscitation.

questions.question: A 26-year-old woman collapsed, suffered cardiac arrest, and remained in a persistent vegetative state with a feeding tube for 15 years. She had no advance directive or surrogate designation, so her husband became her guardian, and he and her parents fought for years in court — reaching the governor, Congress, and the President — over removing the tube. What should EMS crews take from this case?
choices: Ask families for any directive or surrogate paperwork on every incapacitated patient, because young, healthy patients are the least likely to have one and the most likely to generate a dispute.
When family members disagree about care, the crew should follow whichever side spoke to them first.
Young, healthy patients do not need directives, so crews need not ask their families for any paperwork.
A legal guardian's decisions for an incapacitated patient can never be challenged by other family members.
questions.explanation: With no written directive, the patient's own wishes had to be guessed at through years of court and political fights.

questions.question: A patient underwent an X-ray study of the aorta and was left with permanent paralysis of his lower legs. He claimed neither he nor his family had been told the details or risks of the procedure, and a jury awarded him $250,000. The appeal in his case coined the term 'informed consent.' What rule came out of it?
choices: Providers should withhold uncommon risks so patients are not frightened away from needed care.
Only the physician performing the procedure, and never any other team member, has a duty to explain its risks.
Consent is fully valid as long as the patient signs the consent form before the procedure begins.
A signature or a 'yes' is not enough: the patient must first hear the material risks, benefits, and alternatives in understandable terms.
questions.explanation: Permission given without disclosure of the facts needed for an intelligent decision is not informed consent.

questions.question: What does the term "false imprisonment" mean?
choices: The confinement of a person without legal authority or the person's consent.
Disclosure of information without proper authorization.
The legal duty of an EMT to notify the appropriate authorities in specific situations, such as suspected child or elder abuse or neglect, injuries caused by weapons or crimes, and attempted suicide.
The phase of a civil lawsuit where the plaintiff and defense obtain information from each other that will help both build their cases.
questions.explanation: false imprisonment: The confinement of a person without legal authority or the person's consent.

questions.question: A woman called 911 with respiratory problems. The first paramedic crew knocked on her door, got no answer, and left; a second crew entered about 41 minutes after the first call and found her dead. The Illinois Supreme Court later abolished the public duty rule in the case. What is the lesson for a dispatched crew?
choices: If no one answers the door, the crew has fully satisfied its duty and may clear.
Once dispatched, treat the call as a duty to that patient: make real entry attempts, coordinate dispatch, and document every step.
A second crew's later arrival cancels the first crew's responsibility for the call.
A crew owes a duty only to the public at large, never to an individual caller.
questions.explanation: Once dispatched, the duty runs to that patient; document entry attempts and coordination with dispatch.

questions.question: A psychiatrist's patient died of an AIDS-related illness after refusing medication, demanding that no notes be taken, abusing alcohol and drugs, and ignoring advice to seek HIV treatment for three years. A jury awarded the patient's estate $850,000, but the trial court never instructed the jury on contributory negligence. What lesson should an EMT take from this case?
choices: Contributory negligence can only be raised when the patient caused a vehicle collision.
A patient's refusal of recommended care can become a legal defense, so document refusals, advice given, and the patient's capacity carefully.
A patient's refusal of care eliminates any need to document the encounter.
Refusals only matter legally if the patient signs a witnessed refusal form at the hospital.
questions.explanation: A patient's own refusal of recommended care may support a contributory negligence defense, which makes careful refusal documentation essential.

questions.question: During a heated call review, an EMT calls his partner 'a complete idiot' in front of the crew, but makes no false claim about the partner's care or conduct. Why is this less likely to be successful slander than accusing the partner of faking run reports?
choices: slander requires a false and damaging statement of fact, not just a spoken insult
slander only applies to statements that are also put in writing
slander requires the insult to be spoken in front of a patient
slander applies only when the statement causes a proven monetary loss
questions.explanation: Slander covers false, damaging factual information spoken about a person; a bare insult with no false factual claim does not meet the definition.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: Legal doctrine that can protect an EMS provider from being sued or that may limit the amount of the monetary judgement (the amount of money that a court of law orders one person to pay to another) against the EMS provider.
choices: slander
governmental immunity
chain of evidence
decision-making capacity
questions.explanation: governmental immunity: Legal doctrine that can protect an EMS provider from being sued or that may limit the amount of the monetary judgement (the amount of money that a court of law orders one person to pay to another) against the EMS provider.

questions.question: An EMT asks why Henrietta Lacks' cells raised questions about consent and fairness in research decades later. Those questions belong to which discipline?
choices: informed consent law
public health policy
bioethics
forensic medicine
questions.explanation: Questions of right and wrong in research and treatment are the subject matter of bioethics.

questions.question: A patient who called 911 for chest pain admits he stopped taking his prescribed heart medication months ago. After he sues the EMS agency for a delayed response, the agency argues his own failure to take his medication contributed to his heart damage. What defense is the agency raising?
choices: sovereign immunity
gross negligence
contributory negligence
assumption of the risk
questions.explanation: The defense claims the plaintiff's own conduct contributed to the injuries he is suing over.

questions.question: You find a 62-year-old man unconscious, apneic, and pulseless after collapsing at a park. No family is present and no DNR is found. Under what type of consent do you begin CPR?
choices: informed consent
substituted consent
implied consent
expressed consent
questions.explanation: An unconscious patient who cannot give consent is treated under the legal assumption he would want life-saving treatment.

questions.question: An unconscious patient's dentures are found broken and his face bruised after a transfer, with no witness able to say what happened while the crew had sole control of him. The plaintiff's inability to show the exact mechanism does not defeat the claim because of what doctrine?
choices: good Samaritan immunity
contributory negligence
sovereign immunity
res ipsa loquitur
questions.explanation: When the instrumentality was in the defendant's exclusive control and the injury ordinarily implies negligence, res ipsa loquitur supplies the inference.

questions.question: Mid-transport, an EMT decides the patient 'looks fine,' stops at the patient's house instead of the hospital, and leaves him on the porch without any medical handover. This best describes what?
choices: involuntary transport
abandonment
false imprisonment
malpractice
questions.explanation: Terminating care unilaterally, without consent and without continuing care by an equal or higher medical professional, is abandonment.

questions.question: A 6-year-old girl was reported missing from her home, and police treated the call as a kidnapping: only her bedroom was cordoned off while family and friends walked freely through the rest of the house. That afternoon her father found her body in the basement, removed tape from her mouth, and carried her upstairs. The case remains unsolved, and the early contamination of the scene is still cited as a major investigative failure. What should EMS providers do at a scene like this?
choices: Limit entry, avoid moving anything not needed for patient care, and tell investigators exactly what they touched or moved.
Move the body to a cleaner area so investigators have room to work.
Let family members remain with the body so the scene stays emotionally calm.
Search the rest of the house themselves to locate evidence before police arrive.
questions.explanation: An unsecured scene and a moved body break the evidence record before collection even begins, and no later documentation can restore it.

questions.question: Assessment in Action: If a patient says he has used heroin recently, who should you tell about this?
choices: You should tell the patient's family members and the responding police officer, but leave it out of your hospital report so the patient is not documented as a drug user.
You should not tell anyone about the heroin use, including the hospital staff, because patient confidentiality prohibits sharing any information about illegal drug use.

You should report the heroin use to the nurse, physician assistant, or physician who accepts transfer of care from you at the hospital. This information will be important to continuity of patient care. As health care providers, we should regard drug addiction as an illness, not a crime. You would not need to notify law enforcement unless there are extenuating circumstances.
You should report the heroin use to local law enforcement as soon as possible, because illegal drug use is a crime that EMS providers are required to report on every call.
questions.explanation: From the book's printed answer key.

questions.question: You arrive at a residence where family found a man in bed unresponsive. He is cold, pulseless, apneic, and his jaw and arms cannot be moved because the muscles are stiff. Under protocol, resuscitation is withheld. What definitive sign of death did you find?
choices: dependent lividity
putrefaction
algor mortis
rigor mortis
questions.explanation: Stiffening of the body muscles after death is rigor mortis, a definitive sign of death.

questions.question: A competent, alert 40-year-old with a fractured leg refuses transport after you explain the risks of bleeding and infection, and he repeats that he understands and still refuses. What principle requires you to honor that refusal?
choices: beneficence
informed consent
patient confidentiality
patient autonomy
questions.explanation: A competent patient has the right to make informed choices about his own health care, including refusing transport.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: Written documentation that specifies medical treatment for a competent patient should the patient become unable to make decisions; also called a living will or a health care directive.
choices: discovery
Good Samaritan laws
health care proxy
advance directive
questions.explanation: advance directive: Written documentation that specifies medical treatment for a competent patient should the patient become unable to make decisions; also called a living will or a health care directive.

questions.question: Your crew gives a sedative to a handcuffed patient based only on a police officer's diagnosis, never takes vital signs or estimates the patient's weight, and does not monitor him afterward. He stops breathing. Which term best describes this conduct?
choices: abandonment
contributory negligence
gross negligence
ordinary negligence
questions.explanation: Skipping assessment, dosing, and monitoring is a willful or reckless disregard for the duty and standard of care, not a simple mistake.

questions.question: An 8-year-old boy's teacher repeatedly reported his visible injuries to the county child abuse hotline, and dozens of complaints reached the child welfare agency, yet he was never removed from the home and was later tortured and killed. You now transport a child with fresh, suspicious injuries and learn a report was already filed last month. What should you do?
choices: Report every new sign of abuse you see, even if you believe a report was already made; repeated, specific reports create the record that forces action.
Report again only if you personally witness the abuse taking place.
Skip the report, since duplicate reports only slow down the agency's response.
Document the injuries in the patient care report and leave any reporting to the hospital social worker.
questions.explanation: Mandatory reporting only protects a child when each professional reports fully; report every new sign, even if a report was already made.

questions.question: In 1992, 79-year-old Stella Liebeck spilled McDonald's coffee in her lap and suffered third-degree burns. Trial evidence showed McDonald's required its coffee to be held at 180 to 190 degrees and had received more than 700 prior complaints of customers being burned, yet kept the same policy. A jury awarded $160,000 in compensatory damages after fault reduction and $2.7 million in punitive damages, later reduced by the judge. What made the punitive award supportable here?
choices: Knowing about hundreds of prior burns and keeping the same policy showed a willful and wanton disregard that punitive damages are meant to punish.
The customer was found partly at fault, which allows a jury to add punishment damages to the award.
McDonald's was a large corporation, so any negligence by it automatically qualifies for punishment damages.
The burns were unusually severe, and severity of injury alone is enough to support punitive damages.
questions.explanation: A pattern of ignored complaints turns an accident into the knowing disregard that supports punitive damages.

questions.question: A jury finds an ambulance company knowingly sent out a unit with failed brakes after three written mechanic warnings, injuring a patient. On top of the patient's medical bills and lost wages, the jury adds $500,000 specifically to punish the company and deter others. What are those added damages called?
choices: liquidated damages
nominal damages
compensatory damages
punitive damages
questions.explanation: Money added beyond compensation to punish intentional or willful and wanton disregard for safety is punitive damages.

questions.question: Police have a combative patient handcuffed face-down on the pavement with an officer's weight on his back, and he suddenly goes quiet. What is the restraint called, and what must you do first?
choices: chemical restraint (sedate him before assessing his breathing)
forcible restraint (leave him prone until he calms down completely)
forcible restraint (reposition and assess airway and breathing immediately)
verbal de-escalation (keep talking until he starts responding again)
questions.explanation: Holding a person so he cannot initiate physical action is forcible restraint, and sudden quiet in a prone restrained patient demands immediate repositioning and airway assessment.

questions.question: During discovery, the defense sends your patient-plaintiff 25 written questions asking about prior injuries, other treating doctors, and each item of damages claimed. She must answer in writing under oath. What discovery tool is this?
choices: motions to compel
requests for admission
interrogatories
depositions
questions.explanation: Interrogatories are the written-question tool of discovery, unlike depositions, which are oral questions.

questions.question: A man was found stabbed to death. His girlfriend claimed an intruder had killed him only minutes before she contacted police, but the coroner, arriving eight to ten minutes after police confirmed the death, found rigor mortis had set in and the body was very stiff, suggesting death two to three hours earlier. Her account collapsed and she was convicted. What is the documentation lesson?
choices: Time-of-death estimation belongs to investigators, so EMS notes about body stiffness have no value.
Crews should bend the body's limbs to test the stiffness before investigators document the scene.
Record on-scene observations of rigor precisely — the time, which muscle groups are stiff, and ambient conditions — because they can become court testimony years later.
Rigor mortis develops within minutes of death, so a stiff body confirms that a killing was very recent.
questions.explanation: The stage of rigor observed on scene is evidence that can fix the time of death and break a false timeline.

questions.question: A conscious, alert patient with chest pain clearly tells you, 'Do not touch me, I refuse.' Your partner says implied consent lets you treat anyway. Is he correct?
choices: Yes — a refusal only counts if it is written and signed
No — implied consent does not override a clear refusal
Yes — an emergency always overrides a patient's stated refusal
Yes — implied consent applies whenever the crew believes treatment is needed
questions.explanation: Implied consent applies only when the patient is unable to give consent; a competent patient's expressed refusal controls.

questions.question: An immigrant passenger stood in line with about 200 other women, watched a ship's surgeon examine arms and vaccinate those without a vaccination mark, and when her turn came she held up her arm without objection and accepted the vaccination. She later sued, but the court held her behavior indicated consent. What does this case teach about expressed consent?
choices: A patient's overt actions can give expressed consent, but silence or confusion is not the same; when in doubt, confirm verbally with the patient and document the response.
A patient's silence or confusion should always be treated as consent to treatment.
Providers must ignore a patient's gestures and act only on written instructions.
Only a signed consent form can ever establish that a patient authorized care.
questions.explanation: Expressed consent can be nonverbal: a provider may be guided by the patient's overt acts and outward manifestations.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: Disclosure of information without proper authorization.
choices: breach of confidentiality
health care directive
expressed consent
emergency
questions.explanation: breach of confidentiality: Disclosure of information without proper authorization.

questions.question: YOU are the Provider (32-year-old man, severe headache): What questions should you ask yourself to help determine whether you can transport this patient against his will?
choices: Ask: Is the ambulance stocked for the trip? Has the patient signed the refusal form yet? Can a police officer ride along to witness the refusal?
Ask: Did the patient call 9-1-1 himself? Has he refused care before? Does his family want him transported even though he is alert and refusing?

Ask: Is the patient competent to make decisions? Is there a threat to the patient or others? Is the patient a minor? Is there a court order? Does the patient have a mental illness that impairs judgment? What does state law allow?
Ask: How far is the hospital? Does the patient have insurance? Will the crew be back in service sooner if the patient is transported against his will?
questions.explanation: From the book's printed YOU are the Provider summary.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: Permission to render care.
choices: emergency doctrine
patient autonomy
consent
in loco parentis
questions.explanation: consent: Permission to render care.

questions.question: What does the term "emancipated minor" mean?
choices: Unlawfully touching a patient or providing emergency care without consent.
The manner in which principles of ethics are incorporated into professional conduct.
A person who is under the legal age in a given state but, because of other circumstances, is legally considered an adult.
A term relating to medical jurisprudence (law) or forensic medicine.
questions.explanation: emancipated minor: A person who is under the legal age in a given state but, because of other circumstances, is legally considered an adult.

questions.question: A 68-year-old with a gangrenous toe is alert, explains back to you that refusing amputation could kill her, and calmly refuses transport twice. Her son insists she is 'not thinking straight.' How should you classify her?
choices: incompetent
competent
lacking decision-making capacity
a candidate for involuntary transport
questions.explanation: She understands her condition and the consequences and reasons rationally about her own well-being, so she is competent and may refuse.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: Damages that are sometimes awarded in a civil lawsuit when the conduct of the defendant was intentional or constituted a willful and wanton disregard for the safety of the public and the rights of others.
choices: punitive damages
rigor mortis
discovery
medicolegal
questions.explanation: punitive damages: Damages that are sometimes awarded in a civil lawsuit when the conduct of the defendant was intentional or constituted a willful and wanton disregard for the safety of the public and the rights of others.

questions.question: Which patient is an emancipated minor?
choices: A 17-year-old who works part time after school and lives at home
A 17-year-old active-duty service member living independently
A 16-year-old high school student who lives with both parents
A 15-year-old who states she feels mature enough to decide on her own
questions.explanation: Military service and independent living are classic circumstances that make an underage person legally an adult.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: A written document that specifies medical treatment for a competent patient, should he or she become unable to make decisions in the future; also known as an advance directive or a living will.
choices: false imprisonment
negligence
health care directive
Good Samaritan laws
questions.explanation: health care directive: A written document that specifies medical treatment for a competent patient, should he or she become unable to make decisions in the future; also known as an advance directive or a living will.

questions.question: Dispatch sends you to a school bus rollover with 18 injured children, several unconscious and one with uncontrolled leg bleeding. This situation, threatening the welfare of a group and requiring immediate intervention, is best defined as a(n):
choices: disaster
emergency
urgent situation
mass-casualty incident
questions.explanation: A serious situation threatening the life or welfare of a group and requiring immediate intervention is an emergency.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: Type of consent in which a patient who is unable to give consent is given treatment under the legal assumption that he or she would want treatment.
choices: competent
implied consent
health care proxy
false imprisonment
questions.explanation: implied consent: Type of consent in which a patient who is unable to give consent is given treatment under the legal assumption that he or she would want treatment.

questions.question: A new EMT asks why the crew spends so long writing a neat, complete, accurate report after every call instead of just noting the basics. The best answer is that the report is a legal document that stands as the record of the care provided. What is this record called?
choices: run summary log
incident report
patient care documentation
quality assurance review
questions.explanation: The patient care report is the written or electronic legal record of the call and of the care given.

questions.question: Why do EMS agencies retain run reports for many years after a call involving a young child?
choices: HIPAA rules — pediatric records must simply be kept until the patient turns eighteen
Good Samaritan laws — they protect the crew only while the injured child is still a minor
statute of limitations — the filing period may not begin or may be tolled until the child reaches adulthood
mandatory reporting rules — claims involving children have no filing deadline at all
questions.explanation: Because the time within which a case must be commenced can be paused for minors, claims from one call can be filed years later.

questions.question: Two adult children argue at the bedside of their unresponsive mother, and neither can produce any advance directive or proxy paperwork. What is the EMT's best action?
choices: implied consent does not apply (withhold care until a court appoints a decision-maker)
living will (search the home for any written wishes before providing treatment)
health care proxy (the older child automatically becomes the agent; follow her instructions)
health care proxy (none produced; treat under implied consent/emergency care and let the facility and courts sort out decision-making authority)
questions.explanation: Without an appointed proxy, the crew should provide emergency care and transport rather than letting an unverified family dispute delay treatment.

questions.question: After a dramatic rescue, you post a photo of the injured patient on your personal social media account without the patient's permission. Which federal law have you most likely violated?
choices: The Communications Decency Act
EMTALA
The Freedom of Information Act
HIPAA
questions.explanation: Posting an identifiable patient's image is an unauthorized disclosure of protected health information under HIPAA.

questions.question: You find a patient with no pulse or breathing whose purple-red discoloration is fixed across the front of the chest and face, yet the body is lying on its back. What is this discoloration called?
choices: algor mortis
rigor mortis
putrefaction
dependent lividity
questions.explanation: Blood settling to the lowest point of the body causes the discoloration, and its fixed pattern here shows the body was face down earlier.

questions.question: What does the term "health care proxy" mean?
choices: Damages awarded in a civil lawsuit that are intended to restore the plaintiff to the same condition that he or she was in prior to the incident complained about in the lawsuit.
Failure to provide the same care that a person with similar training would provide.
The philosophy of right and wrong, of moral duties, and of ideal professional behavior.
A type of advance directive executed by a competent adult that appoints another individual to make medical treatment decisions on his or her behalf when he or she is unable to do so.
questions.explanation: health care proxy: A type of advance directive executed by a competent adult that appoints another individual to make medical treatment decisions on his or her behalf when he or she is unable to do so.

questions.question: In 2008, a 48-year-old man with chest pain and shortness of breath was walked down three flights of stairs by paramedics, but his patient care report stated he had been carried down in a stair chair. His daughter spotted the false entry in his records, both paramedics admitted the stair chair was never used, and both were fired after a state investigation. What rule of documentation did they break?
choices: EMTs must document only what was actually done; a report that describes care never given is falsification, with legal and career consequences.
Minor exaggerations in a report are acceptable when the overall care was appropriate.
The report should describe the care that protocol says should have been given on the call.
In court, only the patient's outcome matters, not whether the report was accurate.
questions.explanation: The falsified report, not just the care, drove the firings and the state investigation; once the record was proven false, the service's account of the whole call collapsed.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: The confinement of a person without legal authority or the person's consent.
choices: negligence per se
abandonment
rigor mortis
false imprisonment
questions.explanation: false imprisonment: The confinement of a person without legal authority or the person's consent.

questions.question: In the 1995 O.J. Simpson murder trial, there were no eyewitnesses and no murder weapon, so the prosecution's case rested heavily on forensic evidence: DNA matches on blood near the victims, on a glove, and in a vehicle, plus autopsy testimony from the chief medical examiner. The defense attacked how samples were collected and whether they were contaminated, and the jury acquitted. What lesson does this hold for an EMT on a potential crime scene?
choices: Avoid documenting scene details in the run report, because written records only create legal exposure.
Preserve evidence, limit traffic through the scene, and document who touched what, because EMS actions become medicolegal evidence.
Move or clean up items freely once patient care is done, since forensic teams only use what they collect themselves.
Collect any suspected evidence into one bag so investigators can sort it out at the laboratory.
questions.explanation: Chain of custody and scene preservation by EMS can decide whether forensic evidence survives legal challenge.

questions.question: A patient with chest pain says, 'Just take me in, don't explain anything.' The crew explains the risk of sudden death from refusing the cardiac monitor and aspirin, and the patient then accepts both. The crew's explanation was required to establish what?
choices: involuntary consent
implied consent
informed consent
substituted consent
questions.explanation: Explaining material risks, benefits, and alternatives before the competent patient gives permission is what makes the consent informed.

questions.question: Elizabeth Bouvia, 28, had severe cerebral palsy and quadriplegia when hospital staff inserted a nasogastric feeding tube against her will; in 1986 a California court found she was intelligent and mentally competent, understood the consequences of refusing the tube, and ordered it removed. What rule for EMTs follows from her case?
choices: A patient who needs a feeding tube is automatically unable to make her own treatment decisions.
Disability is not incompetence; a competent patient's refusal stands even when the crew believes the choice will shorten life.
When a patient is severely disabled, family members rather than the patient make treatment decisions.
Providers may override a patient's refusal whenever refusing treatment will shorten the patient's life.
questions.explanation: The court protected Bouvia's refusal precisely because she was competent — able to make rational decisions about her own well-being.

questions.question: An EMT fails to give oxygen to a hypoxic patient, but expert testimony shows the patient died instantly from an unrelated massive stroke that oxygen could not have affected. Which element will the plaintiff most likely fail to prove?
choices: duty
breach of duty
damages
proximate causation
questions.explanation: Without a causal connection between the breach and the death, proximate causation is not established.

questions.question: A competent 68-year-old signs a written document stating she does not want to be placed on a ventilator or receive tube feeding if she becomes unable to make decisions. What is this document called?
choices: a medical release of information form
health care directive
an informed consent form
a do not resuscitate (DNR) order
questions.explanation: A written document specifying treatment for a competent patient who later cannot decide is a health care directive, also called an advance directive or living will.

questions.question: A former volunteer firefighter sued for defamation, alleging that a former mayor's wife falsely accused him on Facebook of threatening her and her teenage son, and that a former councilwoman repeated the allegations online and in a resignation letter. Police investigated the encounter and filed no charges. Why would these claims be libel rather than slander?
choices: Facebook posts count as spoken words, so written claims about them are slander.
A false statement is libel only when it appears in a printed newspaper.
Online accusations cannot be defamation because the author can delete them.
The accusations were communicated in writing, in Facebook posts and a resignation letter, and false written statements that damage a reputation are libel.
questions.explanation: A Facebook post is a written publication that can be screenshotted and filed in court.

questions.question: Your county-run ambulance crew is sued after a patient claims a delayed response harmed him. The county's lawyer argues the service is a governmental function and the claim should be dismissed before trial. What doctrine is the lawyer using?
choices: Good Samaritan protection
statute of limitations
qualified immunity
governmental immunity
questions.explanation: Governmental immunity is the legal doctrine that can protect a government EMS provider from being sued or limit the judgment against it.
