questions.question: Navigate Case Study (32-year-old man, low blood glucose): What is the difference between informed and implied consent, and why is obtaining patient consent so important?
choices: Informed consent is permission from a competent patient after you explain the treatment, its risks and benefits, and the alternatives. Implied consent is assumed in an emergency when the patient is unconscious or otherwise unable to consent and a reasonable person would want care. Obtaining consent respects the patient's legal right to decide about his own care, and treating without it can be considered battery.

Informed consent is granted by medical control over the radio, while implied consent is granted by family members at the scene. Consent is important mainly as documentation for the patient care report.

Informed consent is a signed written form used at the hospital, while implied consent is a verbal yes from a conscious patient. Consent matters mainly so the agency can bill the patient for treatment and transport.

Informed consent applies to minors with a parent present, while implied consent applies to any adult who called 9-1-1. Consent is important because it allows the crew to share the patient's information with bystanders.
questions.explanation: Answer written from the chapter (no printed key).

questions.question: What does the term "proximate causation" mean?
choices: The seizing, confining, abducting, or carrying away of a person by force, including transporting a competent adult for medical treatment against his or her will.
When a person who has a duty abuses it, and causes harm to another individual, the EMT, the agency, and/or the medical director may be sued for negligence.
A theory that may be used when the conduct of the person being sued is alleged to have occurred in clear violation of a statute.
Permission to render care.
questions.explanation: proximate causation: When a person who has a duty abuses it, and causes harm to another individual, the EMT, the agency, and/or the medical director may be sued for negligence.

questions.question: A school district required random drug testing of student athletes after a rise in drug use, and the Supreme Court upheld the program, emphasizing the schools' custodial and tutelary responsibility for children in their charge. What does this mean for an EMT on a school call?
choices: A school's responsibility for its students ends at the classroom door.
School staff carry no legal responsibility for students during the school day.
Schools may never impose any health or safety requirements on their students.
Schools standing in loco parentis may impose health and safety requirements on students in their care, so coordinate with the school nurse and staff who hold that responsibility.
questions.explanation: Schools may impose health and safety requirements on students in their care; coordinate with school nurses and staff who hold that responsibility.

questions.question: On a disaster scene, an EMT must decide which of two critical patients gets the only available ambulance, applying the triage principle of doing the greatest good for the greatest number. Putting that ethical principle into her professional conduct is an example of:
choices: ethical theory
professional etiquette
moral reasoning
applied ethics
questions.explanation: Applied ethics is the manner in which principles of ethics are incorporated into professional conduct.

questions.question: An EMT-B is riding with a paramedic partner when a critical patient needs an IV medication. The paramedic is busy with the airway and says, 'You start the IV and push it, you've watched me do it plenty of times.' What should the EMT-B do?
choices: perform it this one time and document that the paramedic directed it
start the IV line but let the paramedic push the medication
start the IV only because the patient is critical and no one else is free
refuse; IV medication administration is outside the EMT-B scope of practice
questions.explanation: Scope of practice is set by state law for each certification level, and a partner's instruction cannot expand what an EMT-B is legally able to do.

questions.question: In Aurora, Colorado in 2019, paramedics were called for 23-year-old Elijah McClain, who had been restrained by police after a suspicious-person call and had committed no crime. Without performing a physical assessment, the paramedics gave him 500 mg of ketamine for 'excited delirium' even though he weighed about 143 pounds, a weight for which a weight-based dose would have been about 325 mg. He stopped breathing, went into cardiac arrest, and died days later. What does this case teach the EMT?
choices: A standard adult sedative dose is acceptable for any patient as long as the drug is given by the approved route.
Sedation decisions on a police scene belong to the officers, so the EMT should administer the dose they request without delay.
Once a patient is handcuffed, monitoring can wait until arrival at the hospital because the patient is secure.
Assess the patient yourself, verify weight before giving weight-based drugs, and monitor the patient after sedation; deferring to police is not a defense.
questions.explanation: Skipping assessment, weight verification, and monitoring after sedation is a reckless disregard of the standard of care.

questions.question: On a dark night in 1915, a car collides with a horse-drawn buggy, killing its driver. The buggy was being driven without the lights New York's Highway Law required after dark. The trial judge told jurors the missing lights were only some evidence of negligence, but the Court of Appeals reversed, holding the unexcused omission of the statutory lights was negligence in itself. What principle does this case establish for an ambulance operator?
choices: A statutory violation is only minor evidence that a jury is free to disregard whenever it wishes.
Equipment requirements in a statute are guidelines that carry no legal weight in a negligence case.
The driver of the motor vehicle is automatically liable for any nighttime collision, regardless of the law.
Traffic statutes on lights, signals, and speed set the legal standard of care, and a jury may not be allowed to excuse a clear violation.
questions.explanation: A clear, unexcused statutory violation can establish negligence as a matter of law rather than serving as mere evidence.

questions.question: At the station, an EMT loudly tells two coworkers and a patient's family member that a rival paramedic 'shows up drunk on half his shifts,' which is not true, and the paramedic is passed over for a promotion. What tort has the EMT most likely committed?
choices: libel
negligence
breach of patient confidentiality
slander
questions.explanation: False, damaging information about a person communicated by spoken word to third parties is slander.

questions.question: What does the term "informed consent" mean?
choices: Permission for treatment given by a competent patient after the potential risks, benefits, and alternatives to treatment have been explained.
A term relating to medical jurisprudence (law) or forensic medicine.
The written or electronic legal record of an EMS call, which courts treat as a reflection of the care itself, so that an incomplete or untidy report is read as evidence of inadequate care.

Statutory provisions enacted by many states to protect citizens from liability for errors and omissions in giving good faith emergency medical care, unless there is wanton, gross, or willful negligence.
questions.explanation: informed consent: Permission for treatment given by a competent patient after the potential risks, benefits, and alternatives to treatment have been explained.

questions.question: An EMT responding to a murder scene photographs the victim's body on his cell phone and posts the photo on his Facebook page. He is fired, his certification is revoked, and he is barred from ever working as an EMT again. What rule did he break?
choices: Scene photos are acceptable as long as the patient's face is not visible
Photos may be shared if they are posted to a private social media account
Posting is allowed once the call is over and the patient is deceased
Never photograph a patient or scene for personal use; posting it discloses patient information with no authorization and can end a certification.
questions.explanation: One personal post of a patient or scene photo is a breach of confidentiality that can end a certification and become a criminal case.

questions.question: Paramedics treating a restrained 23-year-old give 500 mg of ketamine without basic checks such as taking a pulse; experts say the dose was too high for his roughly 143 pounds, and he suffers cardiac arrest and dies. What should the paramedics have done?
choices: Assess the patient yourself, verify weight-based dosing, and never let a police diagnosis replace your own medical evaluation.
Give the standard adult ketamine dose without checking the patient's weight.
Rely on the police account of the patient's behavior when choosing a sedative.
Sedate first and take vital signs once the patient is calm and restrained.
questions.explanation: Your own assessment and verified weight-based dosing are required; a police diagnosis never replaces your medical evaluation.

questions.question: After a dramatic MVC, an EMT posts on social media: 'Bad wreck on Route 7 tonight, driver didn't make it,' with no name. A local reporter identifies the patient from the details. What has the EMT committed?
choices: negligence
defamation
breach of confidentiality
libel
questions.explanation: Details that let others identify the patient disclose patient information without proper authorization, even without a name.

questions.question: A city EMS system and a private ambulance company provide identical care on identical calls. A negligence suit against the city system is dismissed on immunity grounds while the suit against the private company proceeds. Why the difference?
choices: governmental immunity
Good Samaritan protection
qualified immunity
vicarious liability
questions.explanation: Governmental immunity generally applies to EMS systems operated by municipalities or other governmental entities, not to private companies.

questions.question: A volunteer responder at a scene deliberately ignores obvious signs of a tension pneumothorax, jokes that the patient can wait, and provides no care at all out of indifference. Why might Good Samaritan protection fail?
choices: scope of practice (the responder was not certified to assess chest injuries)
implied consent (the patient could not consent, so no protection can apply)
Good Samaritan laws (they never protect volunteer responders at a scene)
Good Samaritan laws (gross/wanton negligence exception)
questions.explanation: The statutes do not protect wanton, gross, or willful negligence, and indifference to an obvious life threat can meet that standard.

questions.question: What does the term "duty to act" mean?
choices: Written, accepted levels of emergency care expected by reason of training and profession; written by legal or professional organizations so that patients are not exposed to unreasonable risk or harm.
A medicolegal term relating to certain personnel who either by statute or by function have a responsibility to provide care.
Unilateral termination of care by the EMT without the patient's consent and without making provisions for continuing care by a medical professional who is training at the same level or higher.
Written documentation that specifies medical treatment for a competent patient should the patient become unable to make decisions; also called a living will or a health care directive.
questions.explanation: duty to act: A medicolegal term relating to certain personnel who either by statute or by function have a responsibility to provide care.

questions.question: A barrel of flour falls from the window of a warehouse onto a man passing below, injuring him. He cannot prove exactly how the barrel came to fall or identify the specific careless act involved. The court holds the accident itself is evidence of negligence, because barrels do not roll out of warehouses without carelessness. What principle does this case establish?
choices: Falling objects are legally presumed to be the fault of the injured passerby.
A plaintiff must always prove the precise negligent act before recovering damages.
An injury that ordinarily happens only through carelessness can itself support an inference of negligence, even when the plaintiff cannot demonstrate exactly how it occurred.
Liability for an accident requires a written contract between the parties.
questions.explanation: This is the origin of res ipsa loquitur: liability can be inferred when the plaintiff cannot demonstrate exactly how the injury occurred.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: A medicolegal term relating to certain personnel who either by statute or by function have a responsibility to provide care.
choices: duty to act
bioethics
patient autonomy
proximate causation
questions.explanation: duty to act: A medicolegal term relating to certain personnel who either by statute or by function have a responsibility to provide care.

questions.question: What does the term "battery" mean?
choices: Decomposition of body tissues; a definitive sign of death.
Ability to understand and process information and make a choice regarding appropriate medical care.
Unlawfully touching a patient or providing emergency care without consent.

Damages that are sometimes awarded in a civil lawsuit when the conduct of the defendant was intentional or constituted a willful and wanton disregard for the safety of the public and the rights of others.
questions.explanation: battery: Unlawfully touching a patient or providing emergency care without consent.

questions.question: Assessment in Action: Suppose your partner had introduced himself and asked permission to examine the patient. If the patient nodded and extended his arm, this would be considered:
choices: mature consent.
implied consent.
informed consent.
expressed consent.
questions.explanation: From the book's printed answer key.

questions.question: A young woman was left in a persistent vegetative state after a car crash, sustained by a feeding tube. She had no living will. Her parents asked the hospital to withdraw the tube, but the state required clear and convincing evidence of her own wishes, and the dispute reached the U.S. Supreme Court. What is the main lesson for field providers?
choices: A written directive made while a patient is competent prevents years of litigation; in the field, honor and document any directive the family produces.
Court proceedings are the preferred way to settle a patient's treatment wishes, ahead of any document.
A patient who left no directive is presumed to want all treatment stopped as soon as possible.
Families may withdraw life support on request at any time, with no evidence of the patient's own wishes needed.
questions.explanation: Without a health care directive, proving an incapacitated patient's wishes can take years of litigation.

questions.question: Before starting an IV, you explain the procedure to your alert patient and she says, 'Okay, go ahead.' What have you just obtained?
choices: consent (expressed consent)
an advance directive
informed refusal
implied consent
questions.explanation: Consent is permission to render care, and her verbal authorization gives it.

questions.question: Which of the following is the correct way to share an interesting case with your class instructor?
choices: post it in a closed class group using only the patient's initials
discuss it with all identifying information removed (no breach of confidentiality)
share the full run report as long as it is used for teaching purposes
remove the patient's name but keep the address, date, and location of the call
questions.explanation: Teaching discussion is permitted only when the patient cannot be identified; sharing identifiable details without authorization is a breach of confidentiality.

questions.question: What does the term "forcible restraint" mean?
choices: Blood settling to the lowest point of the body, causing discoloration of the skin; a definitive sign of death.
The act of physically preventing an individual from initiating any physical action.
Disclosure of information without proper authorization.
Refers to the legal responsibility of a person or organization to take on some of the functions and responsibilities of a parent.
questions.explanation: forcible restraint: The act of physically preventing an individual from initiating any physical action.

questions.question: Your patient is unresponsive after a cardiac arrest and cannot speak. His wife hands you a signed living will stating he does not want to be kept alive on machines if there is no hope of recovery. What is this document called?
choices: do not resuscitate order
durable power of attorney for health care
informed consent form
advance directive
questions.explanation: It is written documentation, made while competent, specifying treatment if the patient later becomes unable to make decisions.

questions.question: Two EMTs responded to a domestic dispute involving an allegedly intoxicated man. Police said he needed to go to the hospital, but he said he did not want to be touched and refused. One EMT called his supervisor, who advised against transporting the man against his will, and the EMT told the sergeant his training taught him a forced transport would be considered kidnapping. The EMTs refused to transport him. What should you do when police pressure you to take a refusing, competent patient?
choices: Call your supervisor and medical control and document the refusal, because an order from police does not make a forced transport legal.
Refuse and leave without documenting, because the refusal is the police department's problem.
Transport the patient, because apparent intoxication always overrides a refusal.
Transport the patient, because police on scene can consent on the patient's behalf.
questions.explanation: A police order does not make a forced transport legal; involve your supervisor and medical control and document the refusal.

questions.question: What does the term "emergency" mean?
choices: The manner in which principles of ethics are incorporated into professional conduct.
Written, accepted levels of emergency care expected by reason of training and profession; written by legal or professional organizations so that patients are not exposed to unreasonable risk or harm.
A serious situation, such as injury or illness that threatens the life or welfare of a person or group of people and requires immediate intervention.
Written documentation by a physician giving permission to medical personnel not to attempt resuscitation in the event of cardiac arrest.
questions.explanation: emergency: A serious situation, such as injury or illness that threatens the life or welfare of a person or group of people and requires immediate intervention.

questions.question: What does the term "interrogatories" mean?
choices: When a person who has a duty abuses it, and causes harm to another individual, the EMT, the agency, and/or the medical director may be sued for negligence.
A written document that specifies medical treatment for a competent patient, should he or she become unable to make decisions in the future; also known as an advance directive or a living will.
Written questions that the defense and plaintiff send to one another.
Written documentation by a physician giving permission to medical personnel not to attempt resuscitation in the event of cardiac arrest.
questions.explanation: interrogatories: Written questions that the defense and plaintiff send to one another.

questions.question: In 2020, responders worked a 20-year-old woman for about 30 minutes and a physician pronounced her dead by phone; funeral home staff later found her alive in a body bag. State regulators found the lead paramedic had given the physician inaccurate vital sign information, stopped resuscitation six minutes before he had permission, and changed his report when it was uploaded a second time the next day. Both paramedics' licenses were suspended. What does the altered report teach about patient care documentation?
choices: Never alter a submitted report without a transparent, dated correction; an unexplained change reads in court as a cover-up.
Correcting a report the next day is acceptable as long as the final version looks consistent.
Reports may be rewritten after a bad outcome to clarify what the crew intended to do.
Only the first version of a report can ever be used against a provider in court.
questions.explanation: The altered and inaccurate report became central evidence against the crew: what was documented, and then changed, showed the care did not match the record.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: Cooling of the body after death until it matches the ambient temperature.
choices: chain of evidence
algor mortis
standard of care
contributory negligence
questions.explanation: algor mortis: Cooling of the body after death until it matches the ambient temperature.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: Able to make rational decisions about personal well-being.
choices: bioethics
protected health information
consent
competent
questions.explanation: competent: Able to make rational decisions about personal well-being.

questions.question: Your crew arrives at a man who was struck by a car. Your partner glances at him, takes no vital signs, and clears the scene in under two minutes. The man later dies of internal bleeding a full assessment would have flagged. What is the partner's failure called?
choices: negligence
battery
breach of confidentiality
abandonment
questions.explanation: Negligence is failure to provide the same care a person with similar training would provide, and a similarly trained EMT would have fully assessed the patient.

questions.question: Two bodies are found at the same scene, one in a refrigerated room and one in a warm room. Why will the refrigerated body feel cold much sooner, and why does that limit time-of-death estimates?
choices: putrefaction (decomposition slows the longer a body stays warm)
algor mortis (cooling proceeds until the body matches ambient temperature, so environment changes the rate)
livor mortis (blood settles faster in a refrigerated body)
rigor mortis (muscle stiffening finishes sooner in a cold room)
questions.explanation: Algor mortis ends when body and ambient temperatures match, so a cold environment cools a body faster and makes cooling alone an unreliable clock.

questions.question: A crew member photographs an unconscious celebrity patient to share with friends. Even before any law is cited, what standard condemns this?
choices: duty to act
negligence law
ethics
scope of practice
questions.explanation: Respecting patient dignity and confidentiality is a matter of right and wrong and ideal professional behavior — ethics.

questions.question: A newly certified EMT wants to perform a skill he practiced in a hospital job but that does not appear in his state's EMT protocols or scope. What is the correct course?
choices: perform it once and report it to the state afterward
perform it only while a paramedic watches him do it
do not perform it as an EMT; it is outside his scope of practice
perform it because prior hospital training counts as authorization
questions.explanation: Experience from another job does not change the state-defined scope that outlines the care an EMT may provide.

questions.question: In 1923, James Frye appealed his murder conviction after the trial court excluded results of an early lie-detector test based on systolic blood pressure changes. The D.C. Court of Appeals upheld the exclusion, ruling that a scientific principle must have 'gained general acceptance in the particular field in which it belongs' before expert testimony based on it is admissible. That standard governed scientific evidence for about 70 years. What does this case mean for an EMT's work?
choices: Reliability standards apply to physicians' testimony but never to records created by EMS crews.
Courts evaluate medical evidence only by whether it helped the patient, never by scientific acceptance.
Any test a provider believes is accurate can be presented in court, whether or not the field accepts it.
Documentation and device data from a call may be judged by legal standards of reliability, not just clinical usefulness.
questions.explanation: Frye is foundational medicolegal law: medicine and science must meet the legal rules for admissible proof.

questions.question: A nursing home patient in a persistent vegetative state has no written instructions, and her sons disagree about tube feeding. Which document, had she completed it while competent, would have specified her treatment wishes?
choices: physician orders for life-sustaining treatment
durable power of attorney for health care
advance directive (living will / health care directive)
do not resuscitate order
questions.explanation: An advance directive records a competent patient's treatment choices for a future time when she cannot decide.

questions.question: Which finding is a definitive sign of death that lets an EMT, with protocol and medical direction, decide not to start CPR?
choices: putrefaction
dependent lividity
rigor mortis
algor mortis
questions.explanation: Dependent lividity is listed as a definitive sign of death because blood has settled to the lowest point of the body after circulation stopped.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: The seizing, confining, abducting, or carrying away of a person by force, including transporting a competent adult for medical treatment against his or her will.
choices: kidnapping
emergency doctrine
abandonment
scope of practice
questions.explanation: kidnapping: The seizing, confining, abducting, or carrying away of a person by force, including transporting a competent adult for medical treatment against his or her will.

questions.question: A crew delays on scene for 25 minutes with a STEMI patient who then suffers extensive heart damage that cardiologists testify would have been much smaller with prompt transport. The link between the delay and the damage is which element of negligence?
choices: duty to act
breach of duty
proximate causation
standard of care
questions.explanation: Proximate causation is the proof that the breach of duty caused the patient's harm.

questions.question: An 18-year-old's body is found buried on its right side, but her autopsy shows lividity present and fixed on the front surface of the body, except where pressure was applied. What should responders take from this finding?
choices: Conclude from fixed lividity that the body was buried within an hour of death.
Treat lividity location as a routine detail that does not need documentation.
Reposition the body to match the lividity pattern before investigators arrive.
Note the pattern and position of lividity before moving a body; a pattern that does not match the found position is evidence investigators need preserved.
questions.explanation: Fixed frontal lividity showed the body lay face down for hours; a pattern that contradicts the found position must be preserved and documented.

questions.question: Navigate Case Study (32-year-old man, low blood glucose): Can you continue to restrain this patient and/or transport him to the hospital?
choices: Yes, because his blood glucose was dangerously low earlier, which removes his right to refuse care for the remainder of the call.
Yes. Once a patient has been restrained and an IV started, the crew must complete transport, because stopping treatment midway is always considered abandonment.

No. After the dextrose he is alert and oriented to person, place, time, and event, so he has decision-making capacity and the right to refuse transport. Continued restraint or forced transport could be battery and false imprisonment; remove the IV as requested and follow your refusal protocol.
Yes, if a police officer remains on scene, because law enforcement authorization overrides a competent patient's right to refuse transport.
questions.explanation: Answer written from the chapter (no printed key).

questions.question: Which term is defined as: The federal law, enacted in 1996, that protects the privacy and security of a patient's health information and limits how EMS personnel may use or share it.
choices: gross negligence
torts
HIPAA
ethics
questions.explanation: HIPAA: The federal law, enacted in 1996, that protects the privacy and security of a patient's health information and limits how EMS personnel may use or share it.

questions.question: A paramedic skips a full assessment of a patient found unresponsive earlier that night, does not check vital signs, and leaves the patient at home because a family member says he is sleeping it off. Hours later the patient dies of an overdose. Which concept was most clearly breached?
choices: standard of care
scope of practice
medical direction
duty to act
questions.explanation: The crew failed to provide the accepted level of emergency care expected of a person with their training and profession.

questions.question: A woman enters a permanent vegetative state with no written advance directive and no appointed decision-maker; her husband and parents then spend seven years in court fighting over her feeding tube. What should EMS crews do differently on calls like this?
choices: On calls, identify early whether a proxy document exists and who the appointed agent is; absence of one is what turns family disagreement into litigation.
Assume a spouse automatically holds a health care proxy even without any document.
When family members disagree, follow whichever relative is most insistent on scene.
Delay transport until family members reach agreement about the patient's wishes.
questions.explanation: Because she never appointed a decision-maker while competent, courts spent years deciding who spoke for her.

questions.question: Police on scene order you to take a sober, oriented man who is refusing all care. There is no arrest, no psychiatric hold, and he is not a danger to himself or others. Why should you refuse the forced transport and call medical control instead?
choices: refusing a police order would be obstruction
transporting him could be kidnapping
transporting him would be patient abandonment
his refusal is overridden by implied consent
questions.explanation: Seizing and carrying away a competent person by force without legal authority, including for medical treatment, meets the definition of kidnapping.

questions.question: A family files a civil action, not criminal charges, after a medication error harms their father, asking the court to award compensatory damages. This lawsuit arises from what category of wrongful acts?
choices: torts
administrative violations
criminal offenses
contract disputes
questions.explanation: Civil lawsuits for damages arise from torts, as opposed to criminal prosecutions brought by the state.

questions.question: Six months after a lawsuit is filed over a call you ran, your agency's attorney hands you a numbered list of written questions from the patient's lawyer that you must answer under oath and return. What are these questions called?
choices: subpoenas
depositions
affidavits
interrogatories
questions.explanation: Written questions the plaintiff and defense send to one another, answered under oath in discovery, are interrogatories.

questions.question: Which patient should an EMT recognize as obviously dead without beginning resuscitation: one who is cold and stiff, or one whose body is decomposing with tissue breakdown?
choices: putrefaction (the decomposing body)
the cold and stiff body, because stiffness alone proves death
the cold and stiff body, because cold skin is a definitive sign
neither; both patients require a full resuscitation attempt
questions.explanation: Putrefaction is listed among the definitive signs of death that justify withholding resuscitation.

questions.question: An unencrypted laptop holding the electronic records of 500 patients falls off the back bumper of an ambulance and is never recovered. Federal investigators find the service never did a proper risk analysis, and it pays $65,000 with a two-year corrective action plan. What lesson does this case teach?
choices: Records used for transport rather than billing fall outside HIPAA protection
Encrypt every device that carries patient reports and physically secure it in the rig; a lost unencrypted laptop is a reportable breach.
A lost device is only a breach if someone proves the data was actually read
Paper run reports are the only records that count as protected health information
questions.explanation: Information about patients' care that can be linked to them is PHI, and a lost unencrypted device exposes it.

questions.question: A man with chest pain at work felt fine, worried about cost, and tried to refuse further care. Firefighters and ambulance personnel tackled him, strapped him to a gurney when he tried to walk away, and transported him against his will; at the hospital a doctor found nothing wrong. A federal judge let his false imprisonment claim go to a jury. Why?
choices: Responders may restrain a refusing patient whenever they believe transport is in his best interest.
False imprisonment only applies when a patient is held for more than 24 hours.
Without a valid hold, danger to self or others, or incapacity, restraining a refusing competent adult can be false imprisonment.
Any patient who reports chest pain loses the right to refuse transport.
questions.explanation: He was confined and transported without legal authority and without his consent, which is the core of false imprisonment.

questions.question: What does the term "negligence per se" mean?
choices: Immediate care or treatment.
A medicolegal term relating to certain personnel who either by statute or by function have a responsibility to provide care.

Statutory provisions enacted by many states to protect citizens from liability for errors and omissions in giving good faith emergency medical care, unless there is wanton, gross, or willful negligence.
A theory that may be used when the conduct of the person being sued is alleged to have occurred in clear violation of a statute.
questions.explanation: negligence per se: A theory that may be used when the conduct of the person being sued is alleged to have occurred in clear violation of a statute.

questions.question: A New York statute requires pedestrians on a roadway to walk on the left, facing traffic. Two pedestrians instead walk on the right side because the left side carries very heavy Sunday-night traffic, and they are struck by a car. The driver argues their statutory violation bars their recovery as a matter of law, but the Court of Appeals refuses. Why did the violation not establish negligence per se?
choices: Pedestrian safety statutes are advisory and can never support a negligence per se claim.
The driver failed to prove the pedestrians intended to break the law.
The violation was excused because obeying the statute would have put the pedestrians in greater danger than violating it.
The statute did not apply because the accident happened on a Sunday night.
questions.explanation: Negligence per se has a limit: a violation is excused when compliance would create the very danger the statute aimed to prevent.

questions.question: A patient consents to an abdominal examination under anesthesia but expressly refuses surgery. While she is anesthetized, the surgeon removes a fibroid tumor anyway. The court writes that every adult of sound mind has the right to determine what shall be done with his or her own body, and that a surgeon who operates without consent commits an assault. What lesson should an EMT take from this case?
choices: Consent to one intervention is not consent to another; if the patient said no, or never said yes, do not treat beyond what was authorized.
Once a patient signs any consent form, the care team may proceed as it sees fit.
A refusal given before anesthesia becomes invalid once the patient is unconscious.
Consent to anesthesia automatically covers any procedure the surgeon finds necessary.
questions.explanation: Treatment is lawful only with the patient's permission to render that care.

questions.question: What does the term "HIPAA" mean?
choices: Permission to render care.
The federal law, enacted in 1996, that protects the privacy and security of a patient's health information and limits how EMS personnel may use or share it.
Written questions that the defense and plaintiff send to one another.
The legal duty of an EMT to notify the appropriate authorities in specific situations, such as suspected child or elder abuse or neglect, injuries caused by weapons or crimes, and attempted suicide.
questions.explanation: HIPAA: The federal law, enacted in 1996, that protects the privacy and security of a patient's health information and limits how EMS personnel may use or share it.

questions.question: From 2005 to 2008, employees at a large hospital system repeatedly opened the electronic records of celebrity patients they were not treating, just to look. Nothing was ever shared outside the hospital, but federal investigators still found HIPAA violations and the system paid an $865,500 settlement. Why was the employees' conduct a violation?
choices: Employees may view any record at their own facility as long as they do not copy it.
Accessing a patient's record out of curiosity, with no role in that patient's care, is a HIPAA violation even if nothing is ever shared.
Curiosity access is acceptable for training purposes as long as the employee is credentialed.
Viewing a record only becomes a violation if the information is printed or shared outside the facility.
questions.explanation: EMTs should open or discuss a patient's information only when their job requires it; curiosity alone makes the access illegal.

questions.question: A paramedic responded to a victim at an emergency scene and performed a brief visual inspection, described in court as a '60-second examination.' He took no pulse and no blood pressure, left the scene, and the victim died shortly afterward. A jury awarded wrongful-death damages, and the appellate court upheld a gross negligence verdict because the truncated evaluation was an extreme departure from the standard of care. What practice does this case demand?
choices: A brief visual check satisfies the standard of care for any patient who appears stable.
Take vital signs on every patient contact, because a visual once-over is the fact pattern courts use to define falling below the standard of care.
Vital signs are only required once the patient is loaded for transport.
Negligence can only be found when the provider intended to harm the patient.
questions.explanation: Take vital signs on every patient contact; a visual once-over falls below the standard of care.

questions.question: Two EMTs respond to a patient slumped and unresponsive against a car. They stand nearby for many minutes without a primary assessment, vital signs, or oxygen, and the patient dies. A review finds they did not do what any EMT would be expected to do. What is this?
choices: negligence
abandonment
battery
kidnapping
questions.explanation: Failing to perform the basic assessment and care that similarly trained providers would perform is negligence.

questions.question: A woman waiting on a train platform is injured when guards helping a man board a train knock his unmarked package of fireworks loose; it explodes and topples a scale at the far end of the platform onto her. A jury first awards her damages, but the state's highest court reverses, holding the railroad owed her no duty because injury to her was not reasonably foreseeable. What does this case illustrate about negligence claims?
choices: A plaintiff can recover even when the harm was completely unforeseeable to the defendant.
A civil negligence suit cannot succeed unless the defendant acted intentionally.
Any person injured on a defendant's property can automatically recover damages.
Not every bad outcome is an actionable tort; duty, breach, causation, and foreseeable harm all matter in a negligence claim.
questions.explanation: Negligence liability reaches only plaintiffs to whom a duty was owed and whose harm was reasonably foreseeable.

questions.question: An EMT posts on a public social media page that a coworker 'steals narcotics from the rig,' knowing the claim is false. The coworker is suspended and sues. Which tort fits the written post?
choices: slander
libel
invasion of privacy
false imprisonment
questions.explanation: A false, damaging statement published in writing, including online, is libel; spoken false statements would be slander instead.

questions.question: A crew leaves a printed run report with the patient's name, address, chief complaint, and insurance number on the ambulance dashboard in public view. What category of information has been put at risk?
choices: agency property that anyone on duty may review
public information once the run is complete
protected health information
de-identified statistical data
questions.explanation: Health, care, and payment details that can be linked to an individual are PHI whether they are on paper or on a screen.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: Written documentation by a physician giving permission to medical personnel not to attempt resuscitation in the event of cardiac arrest.
choices: health care directive
health care proxy
forcible restraint
do not resuscitate order
questions.explanation: do not resuscitate order: Written documentation by a physician giving permission to medical personnel not to attempt resuscitation in the event of cardiac arrest.

questions.question: A 23-year-old man was restrained by police and placed in carotid holds. Paramedics who responded injected him with 500 mg of ketamine, and he died days later. A grand jury indicted both paramedics, and each faced counts of second-degree assault in addition to homicide charges. What does this case teach about sedating a restrained patient?
choices: Sedating a restrained patient is a use of force against that patient, so the EMT must assess the patient personally and dose by the patient's actual weight.
Once police have restrained a patient, all medical decisions become the officers' responsibility.
Sedation doses for agitated patients should be estimated generously to ensure they work.
A paramedic cannot be charged with assault for medication given at a police request.
questions.explanation: Sedating a restrained patient is a use of force; assess the patient yourself and dose by actual weight.

questions.question: What does the term "health care directive" mean?
choices: A person who is under the legal age in a given state but, because of other circumstances, is legally considered an adult.
Blood settling to the lowest point of the body, causing discoloration of the skin; a definitive sign of death.
A written document that specifies medical treatment for a competent patient, should he or she become unable to make decisions in the future; also known as an advance directive or a living will.
A medicolegal term relating to certain personnel who either by statute or by function have a responsibility to provide care.
questions.explanation: health care directive: A written document that specifies medical treatment for a competent patient, should he or she become unable to make decisions in the future; also known as an advance directive or a living will.

questions.question: A competent adult with severe cerebral palsy and quadriplegia has a feeding tube inserted and maintained against her will to keep her alive; a court orders the tube removed. What principle controls the outcome?
choices: The hospital's judgment overrides a refusal when the patient is severely disabled.
A competent patient's refusal stands even when you believe treatment would save her life; forcing treatment is not rescue.
Life-sustaining treatment may be continued whenever it could extend life by years.
A refusal of feeding can be honored only after a psychiatric evaluation.
questions.explanation: A competent patient may refuse any treatment, even life-sustaining treatment, and that refusal must be honored.

questions.question: A VA hospital treats a veteran's infected leg with neomycin in 1968, and he develops hearing loss. In January 1969 a private physician tells him the hearing loss was highly possibly caused by the neomycin. He does not file his Federal Tort Claims Act suit until 1972, arguing the clock started only when he learned in 1971 that the treatment was improper. The Supreme Court holds his claim is time-barred. When did his filing clock start?
choices: The claim accrued in 1971, when he first learned from a lawyer that the treatment was improper.
The claim accrued in January 1969, when he knew his injury and its cause, not when he later learned the treatment was improper.
The claim accrued on the date he filed suit, since federal claims have no fixed accrual date.
The claim never accrued because his hearing loss developed gradually over several years.
questions.explanation: Deadlines run from when an injury and its cause are known, not from when a lawyer confirms negligence.

questions.question: In Memphis in 2023, EMTs arrived to find 29-year-old Tyre Nichols handcuffed, bloody, and groaning after a police beating, propped against a police car. For about 19 minutes the EMTs provided no treatment at all: no primary assessment, no vital signs, no oxygen, no IV, and no cardiac monitor. Nichols died in the hospital three days later, and both EMTs were fired and had their licenses suspended. What should the EMTs have done?
choices: Wait until officers finish their investigation before touching the patient, to avoid interfering with a police scene.
Ask the officers for a summary of the patient's condition instead of assessing, since the officers were present first.
Begin their own assessment immediately — airway, breathing, vital signs, and monitor — because police custody does not suspend the EMT's duty to the patient.
Limit contact to asking the patient if he wants transport, and document a refusal if he does not answer.
questions.explanation: Doing nothing for a patient in clear distress is a disregard of the most basic duty to act and assess.

questions.question: A competent adult with a minor ankle injury clearly refuses transport, but the crew straps him to the stretcher and takes him to the hospital anyway because 'policy says everyone goes.' What tort has the crew most likely committed?
choices: battery
abandonment
invasion of privacy
false imprisonment
questions.explanation: Confining and transporting a person without legal authority or his consent is false imprisonment.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: Written questions that the defense and plaintiff send to one another.
choices: interrogatories
emergency medical care
battery
Good Samaritan laws
questions.explanation: interrogatories: Written questions that the defense and plaintiff send to one another.

questions.question: Which patient is competent to refuse care: a severely intoxicated man who cannot state where he is, or an alert woman with quadriplegia who articulately refuses a feeding tube?
choices: both patients are equally competent to refuse
neither patient is able to refuse care
competent (the alert woman)
competent (the severely intoxicated man)
questions.explanation: The woman can process information and decide rationally about her well-being; intoxication that prevents understanding removes that ability.

questions.question: An Iowa EMT is suspended in 2024 for acting outside his scope of practice; a coworker reports he did it again a month later, and state records show he had been disciplined in 2014 and 2015 for IV starts beyond his EMT scope. He is fired. What is the lesson?
choices: Only the first out-of-scope act is punished; later ones are a training issue
Performing an out-of-scope skill is acceptable whenever the patient benefits
A skill learned in another job may be used on duty after one supervised success
If a skill is not in your certification level's scope, do not perform it even if you were trained on it somewhere else.
questions.explanation: Starting an IV is an advanced skill outside an EMT's state-defined scope, and repeating it after discipline escalates the consequences to termination.

questions.question: Assessment in Action: Once your ambulance is dispatched to an emergency, you have an obligation to respond. This is known as:
choices: scope of practice.
duty to act.
breach of duty.
mandatory reporting.
questions.explanation: From the book's printed answer key.

questions.question: You are called to a welfare check and find a body that is bloated and green-black, with skin slippage and a powerful odor of decay. Your partner asks if you should start CPR. What finding settles the question?
choices: dependent lividity
algor mortis
rigor mortis
putrefaction
questions.explanation: Decomposition of body tissues is a definitive sign of death, so resuscitation is not indicated.

questions.question: YOU are the Provider (32-year-old man, severe headache): Why is it important to have the receiving nurse sign the PCR?
choices: The nurse's signature confirms the hospital agrees to pay for the ambulance transport, and without it the EMS agency cannot bill for the call.

The nurse's sign-off ensures that a person with equal or higher medical authority has accepted care of the patient. It is important if questions arise later, and failure to appropriately transfer care could be considered abandonment. Documentation should show that you met your obligation to transfer care.
The nurse's signature is only a courtesy; care is legally transferred as soon as the patient is placed on the hospital bed, whether or not anyone signs the PCR.
The nurse signs the PCR to certify that the crew's assessment was correct, which transfers all legal liability for the patient's care to the hospital's insurer.
questions.explanation: From the book's printed YOU are the Provider summary.

questions.question: A 21-year-old dies of cardiac arrest after an acute asthma attack, and his family sues the responding paramedic and EMT for willful and grossly negligent care; a court grants the responders immunity after finding the evidence did not establish willful or gross negligence. What line decides this kind of case?
choices: Good faith care within your training is protected; reckless disregard of a patient's life is the line that loses that protection.
Immunity applies only when the patient survives the call.
On-duty responders can never claim statutory immunity for their care.
Any error in emergency care removes Good Samaritan immunity.
questions.explanation: Immunity held because the alleged errors, even if negligent, did not rise to the gross or willful level the statute carves out.

questions.question: What does the term "discovery" mean?
choices: A type of advance directive executed by a competent adult that appoints another individual to make medical treatment decisions on his or her behalf when he or she is unable to do so.
When the EMT or an EMS system is held liable even when the plaintiff is unable to clearly demonstrate how an injury occurred.
Damages awarded in a civil lawsuit that are intended to restore the plaintiff to the same condition that he or she was in prior to the incident complained about in the lawsuit.
The phase of a civil lawsuit where the plaintiff and defense obtain information from each other that will help both build their cases.
questions.explanation: discovery: The phase of a civil lawsuit where the plaintiff and defense obtain information from each other that will help both build their cases.

questions.question: What does the term "compensatory damages" mean?
choices: A serious situation, such as injury or illness that threatens the life or welfare of a person or group of people and requires immediate intervention.
The seizing, confining, abducting, or carrying away of a person by force, including transporting a competent adult for medical treatment against his or her will.
Damages awarded in a civil lawsuit that are intended to restore the plaintiff to the same condition that he or she was in prior to the incident complained about in the lawsuit.
Permission to render care.
questions.explanation: compensatory damages: Damages awarded in a civil lawsuit that are intended to restore the plaintiff to the same condition that he or she was in prior to the incident complained about in the lawsuit.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: The time within which a legal case must be commenced.
choices: decision-making capacity
standard of care
statute of limitations
proximate causation
questions.explanation: statute of limitations: The time within which a legal case must be commenced.

questions.question: Your state adds oropharyngeal airways and pulse oximetry to the EMT scope but not CPAP. A neighboring state's EMTs use CPAP routinely. On a mutual-aid call in your state, which list governs the care you may provide?
choices: the neighboring state's scope, since its EMTs work the same call
the national registry's recommended skill list
your agency medical director's personal preference
scope of practice (your state's definition for your level)
questions.explanation: Scope of practice is most commonly defined by state law, so your own state's rules for your certification level control.

questions.question: Which patient presentation is rigor mortis rather than a living patient with muscle spasm?
choices: a patient with tetany whose hands are cramped but who is breathing
a hypothermic patient with stiff, shivering muscles and a pulse
a responsive patient whose jaw is clenched during a seizure
rigor mortis (a pulseless, apneic, cold patient whose muscles have stiffened after death)
questions.explanation: Rigor mortis is a definitive sign of death: postmortem muscle stiffening in a patient with no vital signs, not a treatable spasm in a living patient.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: False and damaging information about a person that is communicated by spoken word.
choices: chain of evidence
bioethics
abandonment
slander
questions.explanation: slander: False and damaging information about a person that is communicated by spoken word.

questions.question: A patient's family sues after a medication error. Their lawyer says he will seek extra damages because the paramedic charted a drug as given that was never given, then hid the error. If awarded to punish that intentional conduct, the extra damages are what?
choices: punitive damages
compensatory damages
restitution damages
special damages
questions.explanation: Intentional falsification and concealment show the willful disregard that punitive damages are meant to punish, unlike compensatory damages that repay losses.

questions.question: A 77-year-old widow has gangrene in her foot and lower leg. Doctors recommend amputation without delay. She first agrees, then refuses and keeps refusing, understanding that refusal will likely lead to her death. Her daughter asks a court to override her. What is the correct view of the mother's refusal?
choices: Her earlier agreement to surgery remains binding and can be enforced despite her later refusal.
Her refusal proves she is incompetent, because no rational person would choose death over surgery.
Her daughter, as next of kin, can consent to the amputation over her objection.
Her refusal must be honored, because she understands the information and the consequences; a choice the crew disagrees with is not proof of incapacity.
questions.explanation: A refusal you disagree with is not proof of incapacity; assess whether the patient understands the information and the consequences.

questions.question: A competent patient having an asthma attack clearly refuses treatment, but providers intubate and treat her against her expressed refusal. The state's highest court holds the emergency exception does not override a competent patient's refusal, and that treating a competent person without consent is a battery. What should an EMT do when a competent patient refuses life-saving care?
choices: Restrain and treat the patient first, then document the refusal after arrival.
Override the refusal, because the emergency exception permits treating any life-threatening condition.
Treat the refusal as automatically invalid because the illness itself impairs the patient.
Respect the refusal: assess capacity, explain the consequences, document carefully, and involve medical control rather than forcing care.
questions.explanation: A competent patient's 'no' removes the permission to render care, even life-saving care.

questions.question: A patient agreed to splinting of the left arm. While he is distracted, an EMT also cuts open and examines his uninjured right arm over his objection. The extra examination is an example of what?
choices: assault
breach of duty
malpractice
battery
questions.explanation: Touching beyond the scope of consent, over objection, is unlawfully touching a patient — battery.

questions.question: A woman dies of injuries from a car crash on February 20, 2021, and her sister alleges the county EMS agency unreasonably delayed treating her. The sister does not file her complaint until November 13, 2024. Delaware law requires health care negligence actions to be brought within two years of the injury, and in February 2025 the court dismisses the case. What decided this EMS case?
choices: The court reviewed the crew's care and found the response time was reasonable.
EMS agencies are immune from negligence suits once two years have passed since a call.
The filing deadline restarted when the family hired a new attorney in 2024.
The claim was filed outside the statute of limitations, so the case was dismissed without ever being heard on its merits.
questions.explanation: Patients and families have a hard filing deadline, so run reports must stand on their own when claims arrive long after the call.

questions.question: What does the term "emergency medical care" mean?
choices: Statutory provisions enacted by many states to protect citizens from liability for errors and omissions in giving good faith emergency medical care, unless there is wanton, gross, or willful negligence.
A type of advance directive executed by a competent adult that appoints another individual to make medical treatment decisions on his or her behalf when he or she is unable to do so.
Immediate care or treatment.
Disclosure of information without proper authorization.
questions.explanation: emergency medical care: Immediate care or treatment.

questions.question: YOU are the Provider (32-year-old man, severe headache): Why is it essential that you obtain consent to treat the patient once you arrive?
choices: Consent matters only for invasive procedures such as IVs and medications; basic assessment and vital signs can be performed on any patient without asking permission.
Consent is mainly a documentation requirement; a patient who called 9-1-1 has already given permission for any treatment the crew decides is necessary once they arrive.

The patient has the right to make decisions about his own health care. Treating a patient without consent can be considered battery, and you can be held liable. Consent also ensures the patient understands the treatment and its risks and benefits.
Consent protects the EMS agency's billing rights, because a patient who has not consented cannot legally be charged for treatment or transport.
questions.explanation: From the book's printed YOU are the Provider summary.

questions.question: A 17-year-old with acute leukemia needs blood transfusions. As a Jehovah's Witness, she refuses them on religious grounds, and a court finds clear and convincing proof of her maturity. What is her legal position in a state recognizing the mature minor doctrine?
choices: Her refusal is never valid, because minors cannot make any medical decisions.
The crew should simply transfuse her, because a life threat cancels any refusal.
Her mother's religious beliefs alone decide the question, regardless of the patient's own maturity.
She may, on clear and convincing proof of maturity, exercise the right to consent to or refuse treatment, so her refusal can be legally valid.
questions.explanation: A near-adult minor's refusal can be legally valid in some states; document maturity evidence carefully and involve medical control early.

questions.question: A man undergoes an appendectomy while unconscious under anesthesia and awakes with a new traumatic injury to his shoulder and neck, unrelated to the surgery. He cannot say who caused it or how it happened. The state supreme court allows his claim against the doctors, nurses, and hospital who controlled his unconscious body to proceed. What is the correct understanding of his claim?
choices: The injury is automatically blamed on the operating surgeon alone.
The claim fails because any injury during anesthesia is an expected risk of surgery.
The patient cannot recover because he cannot identify the exact person who injured him.
Under res ipsa loquitur, the providers who had exclusive control of the unconscious patient can be held to explain an injury that ordinarily does not occur without negligence.
questions.explanation: An unconscious patient cannot protect or speak for himself, so unexplained injuries during care are the providers' responsibility to explain.

questions.question: In Aurora, Colorado in 2019, Elijah McClain, 23, was forcibly restrained by police including a carotid hold; paramedics then gave him 500 mg of ketamine — a dose for a much heavier person than his roughly 143 pounds — without a proper assessment, and he stopped breathing, arrested, and died. What must an EMT do when restraining or sedating a patient?
choices: Restraint and sedation are medical acts: assess the patient yourself, dose by actual weight, and monitor airway and breathing continuously afterward.
A standard adult sedative dose is safe for any restrained patient, regardless of the patient's weight.
Once police have restrained a patient, paramedics may sedate him without performing their own assessment.
Sedation doses may be estimated from a patient's apparent size without weighing or assessing him first.
questions.explanation: McClain's death shows restraint and sedation are medical acts requiring your own assessment, weight-based dosing, and continuous monitoring.

questions.question: What does the term "chain of evidence" mean?
choices: Immediate care or treatment.
The documented, unbroken record of everyone who collected, handled, and transferred physical evidence from a crime scene, maintained so the evidence stays usable in court.
Written questions that the defense and plaintiff send to one another.
Permission for treatment given by a competent patient after the potential risks, benefits, and alternatives to treatment have been explained.
questions.explanation: chain of evidence: The documented, unbroken record of everyone who collected, handled, and transferred physical evidence from a crime scene, maintained so the evidence stays usable in court.

questions.question: An EMT confuses two terms: his partner explains that depositions are asked out loud with a court reporter present, while the other tool is answered in writing. Which tool is answered in writing?
choices: interrogatories
cross-examination
voir dire
depositions
questions.explanation: By definition, interrogatories are written questions sent between the parties; depositions are oral.

questions.question: Navigate Case Study (32-year-old man, low blood glucose): What are other considerations to be addressed before you and your partner leave the scene?
choices: Ask the police officer to witness the refusal form, then leave without explaining the risks, since a written signature alone makes the refusal legally complete.
Remove the IV, tell him never to adjust his insulin on his own again, and advise him that he does not need to see a physician unless he becomes unconscious.

Explain the risks of refusing transport and encourage him to eat a meal with substantial carbohydrates so his glucose does not drop again. Encourage follow-up with his physician, involve medical control per protocol, document the refusal with a signed form and witness, and tell him to call 9-1-1 if symptoms return.
Have him sign the refusal form and leave immediately, because discussing food, follow-up care, or the risks of refusal after a patient has refused is not the crew's responsibility.
questions.explanation: Answer written from the chapter (no printed key).

questions.question: Dispatch sends you to a man clutching his chest, pale and sweating, three minutes from your station. The care he needs — assessment, oxygen, aspirin, and rapid transport — is best defined as what?
choices: emergency medical care
preventive care
routine medical care
definitive in-hospital care
questions.explanation: Immediate care or treatment for an acute presentation is emergency medical care.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: The right of a patient to make informed choices regarding his or her health care.
choices: health care directive
patient autonomy
negligence per se
negligence
questions.explanation: patient autonomy: The right of a patient to make informed choices regarding his or her health care.

questions.question: An 81-year-old woman was being transported from a doctor's appointment back to her nursing home when her unsecured wheelchair slid during a hard brake and she was pressed against a metal barrier, suffering leg fractures that required surgery and a major loss of mobility. A jury awarded her $2.45 million. What lesson does this case teach about non-emergency transports?
choices: Compensatory damages are capped at a lower amount for scheduled non-emergency transports.
A patient's age limits the damages a jury can award for transport injuries.
Wheelchair securement is the sending facility's responsibility, not the transport crew's.
Secure every wheelchair and stretcher patient; 'non-emergency' transports generate the same compensatory liability as 911 calls.
questions.explanation: The award compensated her injury, surgery, and lost mobility, and routine transports carry the same liability as emergency calls.

questions.question: A patient with decision-making capacity chooses a treatment option you think is second-best after hearing the risks, benefits, and alternatives. What should you do?
choices: beneficence (override the choice and give the treatment you judge best)
patient autonomy (honor the patient's informed choice)
medical direction (let the online physician choose for the patient)
implied consent (treat the patient's silence as agreement with your plan)
questions.explanation: Autonomy means the informed choice belongs to the patient, not to the provider who would choose differently.

questions.question: Navigate Case Study (32-year-old man, low blood glucose): Why is it essential to adhere to the principles of patient confidentiality?
choices: Confidentiality rules apply only to written records, so anything the crew saw or heard at the scene may be discussed freely with anyone who asks.
Confidentiality is mainly a courtesy to the patient; sharing information with coworkers or friends carries no legal consequences as long as the patient's name is not used.

Patient information is legally and ethically protected under HIPAA and state law. Disclosing it without authorization can bring legal penalties and discipline and destroys patient trust; patients who believe their information stays private are more willing to give an accurate history.
Confidentiality matters only for patients with sensitive conditions such as HIV; routine calls may be discussed with family, bystanders, and the media.
questions.explanation: Answer written from the chapter (no printed key).

questions.question: What does the term "scope of practice" mean?
choices: Most commonly defined by state law; outlines the care that the EMT is able to provide for the patient.
A person who is under the legal age in a given state but, because of other circumstances, is legally considered an adult.
Immediate care or treatment.
Disclosure of information without proper authorization.
questions.explanation: scope of practice: Most commonly defined by state law; outlines the care that the EMT is able to provide for the patient.

questions.question: A diabetic patient whose blood sugar you corrected is now alert, repeats back the risks of refusing transport including death, and still refuses. What does his repeat-back demonstrate?
choices: informed refusal
decision-making capacity
legal competency
medical clearance
questions.explanation: Understanding and processing the information and consequences of a choice is decision-making capacity, so his refusal can be honored and documented.

questions.question: In December 2012, an unencrypted laptop carrying patient care reports fell off the back bumper of a moving ambulance and was never recovered; 500 patients were affected. Federal investigators later found the ambulance company had done no risk analysis and had no security training program, and the company paid a $65,000 HIPAA settlement. What should the EMTs and their service have done to prevent this?
choices: Report a lost device to regulators only if a patient complains about it.
Secure and encrypt laptops and tablets carrying patient reports; an unencrypted device lost from a moving unit is a reportable HIPAA breach.
Wipe the device remotely and say nothing, since there is no proof anyone accessed the data.
Keep paper backup copies of every report in the ambulance so electronic devices are not needed.
questions.explanation: EMTs must secure laptops and tablets carrying patient reports; an unencrypted device lost on the road is a reportable breach.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: A term relating to medical jurisprudence (law) or forensic medicine.
choices: medicolegal
morality
false imprisonment
mandatory reporting
questions.explanation: medicolegal: A term relating to medical jurisprudence (law) or forensic medicine.

questions.question: A famous radio host with progressive dementia had signed a 2007 advance directive granting health care power of attorney to his daughter and stating he did not want life-sustaining procedures if he lost cognitive function. A conflicting 2011 document naming his wife as agent later surfaces, and the two sides fight in court; a judge ultimately upholds the 2007 directive. As an EMT presented with two conflicting documents and two claimed agents, what should you do?
choices: Follow whichever document is most recently dated without involving medical control.
Let the spouse's instructions override the named agent's document.
Do not pick sides; present all the paperwork to medical control and the receiving facility and let them determine the controlling agent.
Refuse to transport until the family settles the dispute among themselves.
questions.explanation: Competing directives and competing agents are for medical control, the facility, and the courts to resolve — not the crew.
questions.topic: durable power of attorney for health care

questions.question: What does the term "slander" mean?
choices: False and damaging information about a person that is communicated by spoken word.
The seizing, confining, abducting, or carrying away of a person by force, including transporting a competent adult for medical treatment against his or her will.
Refers to the legal responsibility of a person or organization to take on some of the functions and responsibilities of a parent.
A type of consent in which a patient gives verbal or nonverbal authorization for provision of care or transport.
questions.explanation: slander: False and damaging information about a person that is communicated by spoken word.

questions.question: A patient consented to surgery on her right ear to remove a polyp and diseased bone. While she was under anesthesia, the surgeon found her left ear in worse condition and operated on that ear instead. The state supreme court held the unauthorized operation was an assault and battery. What limit on consent does this case set?
choices: Once a patient is under anesthesia, the provider may treat any other condition discovered.
Consent to one procedure extends to any similar procedure the provider judges to be more urgent.
Expressed consent covers only what the patient actually authorized; a new intervention, site, or procedure needs its own consent, not an assumption.
Family members who are present during care can expand the scope of the patient's consent for her.
questions.explanation: Consent to one ear and one operation did not authorize surgery on the other ear.

questions.question: An unconscious crash victim's wallet card states she refuses blood transfusion under any circumstances. The crew, knowing of the card, transfuses her en route. Legally, this is best described as what?
choices: negligence
assault
false imprisonment
battery
questions.explanation: Malette v. Shulman held that treatment given against a known refusal is an unlawful touching, which is battery.

questions.question: What does the term "rigor mortis" mean?
choices: A type of advance directive executed by a competent adult that appoints another individual to make medical treatment decisions on his or her behalf when he or she is unable to do so.
The written or electronic legal record of an EMS call, which courts treat as a reflection of the care itself, so that an incomplete or untidy report is read as evidence of inadequate care.
Stiffening of the body muscles; a definitive sign of death.
The federal law, enacted in 1996, that protects the privacy and security of a patient's health information and limits how EMS personnel may use or share it.
questions.explanation: rigor mortis: Stiffening of the body muscles; a definitive sign of death.

questions.question: What does the term "decision-making capacity" mean?
choices: A theory that may be used when the conduct of the person being sued is alleged to have occurred in clear violation of a statute.
Ability to understand and process information and make a choice regarding appropriate medical care.
The phase of a civil lawsuit where the plaintiff and defense obtain information from each other that will help both build their cases.
Stiffening of the body muscles; a definitive sign of death.
questions.explanation: decision-making capacity: Ability to understand and process information and make a choice regarding appropriate medical care.

questions.question: An attorney tells a family, 'Your claim may be strong, but the court will never hear it because the filing deadline passed last month.' The deadline she means is the:
choices: tolling agreement
statute of limitations
discovery rule
statute of repose
questions.explanation: The statute of limitations sets the time within which a legal case must be commenced; after it expires, courts dismiss regardless of merit.

questions.question: A crew is treating a 10-year-old in continuous status epilepticus whose seizure has already lasted 10 minutes. The child's mother, herself a physician, refuses the protocol benzodiazepine because the child previously suffered respiratory arrest from that drug. The crew faces a 20-minute transport and a time-critical seizure that risks permanent brain injury if untreated. What should the crew do?
choices: Delay treatment until a supervisor arrives on scene to decide which course of action to take.
Honor the mother's refusal without question and simply transport, since a parent always has the final say.
Involve medical control early and document the competing risks weighed when a refusal conflicts with a time-critical protocol.
Give the benzodiazepine immediately without involving anyone else, since protocol overrides any refusal.
questions.explanation: When a refusal conflicts with a time-critical protocol, involve medical control early and document the competing risks you weighed.

questions.question: A man alleged in a federal lawsuit that during an acute medical and mental health emergency at his home, fire department and ambulance personnel restrained him and transported him to a hospital against his will, using force to keep him on the stretcher. He stated he was never placed on an involuntary commitment or psychiatric hold, and his complaint alleged kidnapping, claiming the defendants had no legal authority to keep transporting him once he withdrew consent. What principle does his claim rest on?
choices: Consent given at the scene cannot be withdrawn once transport has begun.
Any mental health emergency automatically authorizes involuntary transport.
Applying restraints during transport makes the patient's consent irrelevant.
Consent can be withdrawn mid-transport, and without a legal hold or incapacity, continuing to restrain and carry the patient is the fact pattern sued as kidnapping.
questions.explanation: Consent can be withdrawn mid-transport; without a legal hold, continuing the transport is sued as kidnapping.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: The manner in which principles of ethics are incorporated into professional conduct.
choices: duty to act
applied ethics
interrogatories
contributory negligence
questions.explanation: applied ethics: The manner in which principles of ethics are incorporated into professional conduct.

questions.question: An EMT documents a patient who is obviously dead with 'muscles stiff throughout the body' at 14:00. A detective later asks why that note matters. What is the best answer?
choices: livor mortis (pooling of blood shows the body's position after death)
algor mortis (body cooling alone fixes the exact hour of death)
rigor mortis (its presence and stage help estimate time of death)
putrefaction (decomposition confirms the body was not recently alive)
questions.explanation: Rigor mortis is the postmortem stiffening of muscles, and its stage is used with other signs to estimate when death occurred.

questions.question: Two paramedics transported a 330-pound patient from a hospital to a nursing facility when the gurney tipped on a sidewalk turn and the patient fell face down, dying weeks later. Both crew members gave sworn testimony describing the straps, the sidewalk, and how the patient shifted his weight, and the court resolved the case on that record without a trial. What does this show about depositions?
choices: Depositions are only a formality and are rarely used to resolve a case.
Only the patient's family can be deposed in a wrongful-death case.
Depositions often decide EMS cases before trial, so prepare by reviewing the run report, protocols, and scene details in advance.
Cases are decided at trial, so deposition answers do not need preparation.
questions.explanation: Sworn deposition testimony can supply the entire factual record on which an EMS case is resolved before trial.

questions.question: After a call goes badly, a paramedic quietly rewrites the report to add an intervention that was never performed. Beyond the care itself, what has the paramedic falsified, creating separate criminal and licensure exposure?
choices: quality improvement review
patient care documentation
incident report
medical direction record
questions.explanation: Altering the patient care report is falsification of the legal record of the call, independent of the quality of the care.
